## Algorithm

### How this concept behaves
Finite, repeatable method mapping specified inputs to outputs. Correctness, termination and resource use are separate claims; selecting the nearest visible route does not necessarily find a globally shortest route.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
def linear_find(items,x):
    for i,v in enumerate(items):
        if v==x: return i
    return None
assert linear_find([4,7],7)==1
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Verify empty input, duplicates and missing values. Explain why the first-match rule is part of the algorithm's contract.

## Abstraction

### How this concept behaves
Exposing essential operations while hiding implementation decisions. A file-like interface with read/write methods can be backed by memory or disk, but only if both satisfy the same contract.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
from io import StringIO
stream=StringIO('abc')
assert stream.read(2)=='ab'
assert stream.read()=='c'
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Replace StringIO with an opened temporary text file. Identify observable behaviors that must remain unchanged and ones that may differ.

### Explain a boundary case
For Abstraction, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.

## API

### How this concept behaves
A defined interface by which components request operations and receive results. It includes parameters, errors, authentication and compatibility rules, not merely the URL of a web endpoint.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
def create_task(title):
    if not isinstance(title,str) or not title.strip(): raise ValueError('title')
    return {'id':1,'title':title}
assert create_task('Read')['id']==1
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Specify how the API responds to an empty title and duplicate request. Explain which part belongs to client validation versus server enforcement.


### Glossary: arguments, arrays and syntax trees

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1067.html

# Glossary: arguments, arrays and syntax trees

## Argument

### How this concept behaves
Concrete value supplied at a function call, distinct from a parameter name in the function definition. Positional and keyword arguments can affect how an API evolves.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
def join(left,right): return left+'-'+right
assert join('a','b')=='a-b'
assert join(right='b',left='a')=='a-b'
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Exchange positional argument order and observe the result; then add a keyword-only optional separator.

### Explain a boundary case
For Argument, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.

## Array

### How this concept behaves
Indexed collection whose layout, indexing rules and element types depend on language. A fixed-size C array and a dynamic Python list are not interchangeable concepts.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
items=[8,13,21]
assert items[0]==8
assert items[-1]==21
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Compute memory and mutation implications of an integer array versus a heterogeneous list; test an out-of-range index.

### Explain a boundary case
For Array, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.

## AST

### How this concept behaves
A tree representing parsed program structure rather than source whitespace or comments. Tools traverse AST nodes to analyze expressions, transform code or build diagnostics.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
import ast
node=ast.parse('x=2+3')
assert isinstance(node.body[0], ast.Assign)
assert isinstance(node.body[0].value, ast.BinOp)
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Compare AST dumps of x=2+3 with x = 2 + 3 and explain why formatting does not change the essential tree.

### Explain a boundary case
For Abstract syntax tree, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.

## Asynchronous

### How this concept behaves
Control flow where an operation can suspend while awaiting IO and other tasks may advance. Async syntax alone does not speed up CPU-heavy calculations or guarantee parallel threads.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
import asyncio
async def task():
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return 7
assert asyncio.run(task())==7
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Run two asynchronous sleep tasks concurrently and compare elapsed time with sequential waits; avoid real external services.

### Explain a boundary case
For Asynchronous, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.

## Atomicity

### How this concept behaves
A group of actions appears all-or-nothing at a specified boundary. SQLite transactions offer atomic commit/rollback; a pair of Python assignments is not automatically atomic across services.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO tasks(title) VALUES ('draft');
ROLLBACK;
-- No inserted row should remain.
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Reproduce a failed transaction in a disposable database, then verify both its successful and rejected writes are handled consistently.

### Explain a boundary case
For Atomicity, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.


### Glossary: backtracking and search complexity

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1072.html

# Glossary: backtracking and search complexity

## Backtracking

### How this concept behaves
Search that explores a candidate, rejects it when constraints fail, then restores state to try another path. Useful for Sudoku and permutations but may need pruning to avoid exponential search.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
def choices(xs):
    if not xs: yield []
    else:
        for i,x in enumerate(xs):
            for tail in choices(xs[:i]+xs[i+1:]): yield [x]+tail
assert len(list(choices([1,2,3])))==6
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Add an early constraint forbidding a particular prefix and measure how many branches are pruned.

## Big O

### How this concept behaves
Asymptotic upper bound describing growth with input size, not exact wall-clock seconds. O(n log n) can still be slower than O(n²) for tiny inputs because constants matter.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
def contains(items,x):
    return x in items
assert contains([1,2,3],2)
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Measure membership lookup across increasing list lengths, then compare with a set built beforehand and include the set-construction cost.

### Explain a boundary case
For Big O notation, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.

## Binary search — glossary definition

### How this concept behaves
Search in sorted data by halving the candidate interval each iteration. With N elements there are O(log N) comparisons; an unsorted list violates the precondition.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
def find(a,x):
    lo,hi=0,len(a)
    while lo<hi:
        m=(lo+hi)//2
        if a[m]<x: lo=m+1
        else: hi=m
    return lo if lo<len(a) and a[lo]==x else None
assert find([1,3,5],3)==1
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Trace lo/hi/m for a missing number, then test duplicates and empty arrays against bisect_left.

## Bit

### How this concept behaves
Smallest binary information unit with values 0 and 1. Bit masks encode flags; confusing signed bit interpretation with mathematical integers can change results.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
READ=1;WRITE=2;EXEC=4
permissions=READ|WRITE
assert permissions&READ
assert not permissions&EXEC
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Add EXEC to the mask and remove WRITE. Predict results of &, | and ~ before executing each bitwise operation.

### Explain a boundary case
For Bit, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.

## Boolean

### How this concept behaves
Logical true/false value used for conditions. Python bool is a subclass of int, so isinstance(True,int) is true; strict numeric validation may require type(x) is int.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
assert (2<3) is True
assert isinstance(True,int)
assert type(True) is bool
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Design a JSON schema check where max_items=True must be rejected even though bool behaves numerically as 1.

### Explain a boundary case
For Boolean, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.


### Glossary: branches, buffers and bytes

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1077.html

# Glossary: branches, buffers and bytes

## Branch

### How this concept behaves
Control-flow choice selecting one path based on a condition. A Git branch is a different concept: a movable reference to commit history, not a conditional statement.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
def label(score):
    if score>=50:return 'pass'
    return 'retry'
assert label(50)=='pass'
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Test scores 49 and 50, then compare coverage of both if branches. Explain what testing only one path misses.

### Explain a boundary case
For Branch, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.

## Buffer

### How this concept behaves
Memory region holding data between producer and consumer speeds. Buffers have capacity limits; unchecked writes can corrupt memory in low-level languages.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
from collections import deque
buffer=deque(maxlen=2)
buffer.append('a');buffer.append('b')
assert list(buffer)==['a','b']
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Push a third element and observe bounded deque eviction. Compare overwrite-oldest policy with queue backpressure.

### Explain a boundary case
For Buffer, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.

## Byte

### How this concept behaves
A group of eight bits in modern platforms; file lengths count bytes, while strings may count Unicode code points. UTF-8 characters can require multiple bytes.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
s='Γ'; encoded=s.encode('utf-8')
assert len(s)==1
assert len(encoded)==2
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Compute UTF-8 bytes of ASCII, Greek and emoji, then inspect hex values. Do not split encoded text in arbitrary byte positions.

### Explain a boundary case
For Byte, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.

## Cache

### How this concept behaves
Stored reuse of expensive or remote results. Cache correctness depends on keys, freshness and invalidation; a fast stale value can be less useful than a slower accurate result.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
from functools import lru_cache
@lru_cache(maxsize=16)
def square(n):return n*n
assert square(3)==9
assert square(3)==9
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Inspect cache_info().hits before and after repeated calls. Explain why this cache cannot safely represent changing user permissions.

### Explain a boundary case
For Cache, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.

## Callback

### How this concept behaves
Function passed to another component for later invocation, such as a button handler or completion callback. Execution context, ordering and lifetime belong to the contract.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
def apply(value, callback):return callback(value)
assert apply(4,lambda n:n*2)==8
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Pass two callbacks that produce different outputs and test what happens if the callback raises an exception.

### Explain a boundary case
For Callback, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.


### Cancellation

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1082.html

# Cancellation — a request, not rollback

## Operational definition
Cancelling a task asks cooperative code to stop at an interruption point. It does not roll back database transactions, erase an HTTP request already received or undo a filesystem change already committed. Cancellation also differs from timeout: a caller may stop waiting while a server continues processing. A robust application specifies which cleanup must run, which exception must propagate and how it handles effects that may already have happened.

## Deterministic Python asyncio demonstration
Save as cancel_lab.py and run python3 cancel_lab.py. Events coordinate the test without unreliable arbitrary sleeps. The worker is suspended at a cancellable await, and its finally block signals cleanup. A separate exception checks that cancellation handling does not accidentally swallow unrelated bugs.

~~~python
import asyncio

async def work(started, cleaned):
    try:
        started.set()
        await asyncio.Event().wait()
    finally:
        cleaned.set()

async def failing():
    raise RuntimeError('real failure')

async def main():
    started, cleaned = asyncio.Event(), asyncio.Event()
    task = asyncio.create_task(work(started, cleaned))
    await started.wait()
    assert task.cancel()
    try:
        await task
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError('cancellation not propagated')
    assert cleaned.is_set() and task.cancelled()
    try:
        await failing()
    except RuntimeError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError('unexpected exception was swallowed')
    finished = asyncio.create_task(asyncio.sleep(0, result='done'))
    assert await finished == 'done'
    assert not finished.cancel()  # Cancellation cannot undo completed work.
    print('PASS asyncio cancellation, cleanup, unrelated errors')

asyncio.run(main())
~~~

## What each assertion establishes
started.wait guarantees the worker reached its cooperative suspension point before task.cancel. Awaiting the cancelled task raises asyncio.CancelledError, which must propagate to an appropriate owner. The finally block runs and signals cleaned. A task that has already finished cannot be retroactively cancelled; this example checks that cancel() returns false. If external work was already committed, the application needs an idempotent retry key, reconciliation or compensating action rather than pretending cancellation undoes history.

## Failure drills
1. Remove the finally cleanup and rerun the test; explain why a background lock or file could remain held.
2. Insert a protected resource using a context manager and trace its release when cancellation arrives during await.
3. Replace the failing function with a network mock raising RuntimeError. Catch that error separately; do not turn every exception into cancellation success.
4. Simulate a service accepting a request just before its caller times out. Document what the caller can truthfully know and when status must be checked.

**Evidence:** PASS, a cancellation state trace (created, running, cancelled, cleaned), and a rule for retrying already-committed work.


### Glossary: CI pipelines, command lines and closures

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1083.html

# Glossary: CI pipelines, command lines and closures

## CI

### How this concept behaves
Automated build and test checks on changes. CI increases feedback speed but does not replace review, security assessment or runtime verification on actual target devices.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
python -m compileall -q .
python -m unittest discover -v
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Create an offline test project with one passing and one failing test and observe how CI exit codes indicate failure.

### Explain a boundary case
For Continuous integration, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.

## CLI

### How this concept behaves
Program controlled through arguments and exit status instead of a graphical interface. Good CLIs document input options, distinguish stdout/stderr and return nonzero on failure.

### Work through a small example
~~~text
import argparse
p=argparse.ArgumentParser();p.add_argument('--count',type=int,default=2)
assert p.parse_args(['--count','3']).count==3
~~~

### Investigate the behavior
Try --help and --count wrong, capture stdout/stderr and exit status; document what another script can rely upon.

### Explain a boundary case
For Command-line interface, test a second input that changes the outcome and record the expected behavior before execution. Explain which requirement fails and why the baseline example does not cover it.

## Closure

### Concept in practice
A closure is a function that uses names from the lexical scope in which it was created, even after that outer call returns. In Python a returned nested function holds access to the captured `step` value; rebinding an enclosing variable requires `nonlocal`, but merely reading it does not.

### Focused example
~~~python
def make_adder(step):
    def add(value): return value + step
    return add
plus3 = make_adder(3)
assert plus3(7) == 10
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
Create two adders with different steps and confirm their captured values remain independent. In a loop, investigate late binding of a shared loop variable and fix it with a default argument or a factory.

**Reference:** https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/classes.html#python-scopes-and-namespaces

## Commit

### Concept in practice
A commit is an immutable Git object identifying a tree snapshot, parent commit references and metadata. Its SHA is content-derived; a branch is only a movable pointer to a commit. Committing locally does not publish changes to a remote.

### Focused example
~~~sh
git status --short
git add -- notes.md
git commit -m 'Explain the new test'
git show --stat --oneline HEAD
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
Use a disposable repository to change the same file twice, produce two commits, and compare `git diff HEAD~1 HEAD`. Check that untracked files are excluded unless staged and that `git push` is a separate operation.

**Reference:** https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Internals-Git-Objects

## Compiler

### Concept in practice
A compiler transforms source code into another representation, often machine code or bytecode. Lexing, parsing, type checking, optimization and code generation are distinct stages, and an error in one stage cannot be solved by treating every diagnostic as a runtime problem.

### Focused example
~~~c
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) { puts("hello"); return 0; }
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
Compile the program with warnings, then remove a semicolon to trigger a syntax error. Restore it and replace `puts` with an undeclared function to distinguish a missing declaration from a linker failure. A successful build does not prove correct behavior for all inputs.

**Reference:** https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/


### Glossary: concurrency, conditions and containers

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1088.html

# Glossary: concurrency, conditions and containers

## Concurrency

### Concept in practice
Concurrency means multiple tasks can make progress during overlapping periods; they need not execute simultaneously. Parallelism specifically means execution at the same time on multiple processing resources. Interleaved tasks can still share mutable state and create ordering hazards.

### Focused example
~~~python
import asyncio
async def job(i):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return i * 2
async def main():
    return await asyncio.gather(job(1), job(2))
assert asyncio.run(main()) == [2, 4]
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
Verify that gather returns results in the same input order even if individual jobs complete at different times. Contrast cooperative I/O waits with CPU-heavy work that blocks the event loop; do not assume async code automatically runs on multiple CPU cores.

**Reference:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html

## Condition

### Concept in practice
A conditional chooses a branch using a predicate. Program correctness depends not just on truthiness but on the exact boundary conditions: greater-than differs from greater-than-or-equal, and `None`, empty strings or zero may be coerced to false in ways that obscure meaning.

### Focused example
~~~python
def shipping_cost(total):
    if total < 0: raise ValueError('negative total')
    if total >= 50: return 0
    return 5
assert shipping_cost(49.99) == 5
assert shipping_cost(50) == 0
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
Test exactly below, at and above the 50-unit threshold. Change the order of conditions and explain whether a negative input could be treated as a normal shipping price. Prefer explicit `is None` when missing data differs from numeric zero.

**Reference:** https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#if-statements

## Container

### Concept in practice
An application container packages processes with filesystem layers and runtime settings while relying on the host kernel for isolation. A container is not a virtual machine: it normally shares the host kernel, and its network, users, capabilities and mounts must be configured intentionally.

### Focused example
~~~sh
# On a machine with Docker and a trusted base image:
docker run --rm --network none --read-only alpine:3.20 sh -c 'id; uname -s'
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
On a supported host, compare `uname` inside and outside the container, then inspect which file writes fail with `--read-only`. Never mount your home directory or container engine socket just to make a demo succeed; such mounts change the security boundary.

**Reference:** https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/

## Coroutine

### Concept in practice
A coroutine is a computation whose execution can suspend and later resume. In Python, calling an `async def` function creates a coroutine object; it is not automatically executed to completion. An event loop orchestrates awaits and scheduled tasks.

### Focused example
~~~python
import asyncio
async def answer():
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return 42
assert asyncio.run(answer()) == 42
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
Try `created = answer()` without awaiting and inspect its type; then explicitly close it if the experiment does not await it, so no warning is leaked. Inside an already running event loop use `await`, not a nested `asyncio.run`.

**Reference:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html


### Glossary: data races, deadlocks and debugging

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1092.html

# Glossary: data races, deadlocks and debugging

## Data race

### Concept in practice
A data race occurs when concurrent execution accesses the same mutable location without appropriate synchronization and at least one access writes it. In languages with weakly defined or undefined racy semantics this may invalidate assumptions; in Python thread scheduling still makes multi-step updates non-atomic.

### Focused example
~~~python
from threading import Lock
value = 0
lock = Lock()
def safe_increment():
    global value
    with lock: value += 1
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
Run many safe increments on a shared counter and assert the final count. Then explain why replacing the lock with a `sleep` call would not enforce correctness. For immutable message passing, compare the benefits and overhead with mutex-based shared state.

**Reference:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html#lock-objects

## Deadlock

### Concept in practice
Deadlock means participants wait on resources in a cycle such that none can make progress. Two threads taking locks in opposite orders are a classic example. A slow task or high CPU use alone does not prove deadlock; identify the wait-for cycle before diagnosing it.

### Focused example
~~~python
from threading import Lock
first, second = Lock(), Lock()
def do_work():
    with first:
        with second:
            return 'ok'
assert do_work() == 'ok'
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
Document a global lock acquisition order for every path needing both locks. In a diagram, show the unsafe opposite-order sequence without actually running code that intentionally hangs. Explore bounded lock acquisition timeouts and graceful failure.

**Reference:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html#lock-objects

## Debugging

### Concept in practice
Debugging is the process of finding the mechanism that causes observed behavior to differ from a specification. It is not the same as randomly changing lines until a symptom disappears. A minimal reproducer, expected-versus-actual comparison and a regression test make the diagnosis falsifiable.

### Focused example
~~~python
def average(values):
    if not values: return None
    return sum(values) / len(values)
assert average([]) is None
assert average([2, 4]) == 3
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
Create a failing version that divides by zero for an empty list. State the invariant 'do not divide when the count is zero' and add a regression test before repairing it. For a UI bug, also record browser version and reproduction actions.

**Reference:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/pdb.html

## Dependency

### Concept in practice
A dependency is another component needed to build, run or test your software. Direct dependencies are declared explicitly; transitive dependencies are pulled in by those components. Version ranges, lockfiles and platform compatibility affect whether repeated installs yield the same behavior.

### Focused example
~~~sh
python -m pip --version
python -m pip list --format=freeze
# inspect the local environment; these commands install nothing
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
Compare a pinned and unpinned requirements file in a disposable virtual environment. Record direct packages separately from the full resolved graph. Avoid installing a package merely because its name resembles an error; verify publisher and official documentation.

**Reference:** https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/discussions/install-requires-vs-requirements/


### Glossary: determinism, dictionaries and dynamic types

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1096.html

# Glossary: determinism, dictionaries and dynamic types

## Determinism

### Concept in practice
A deterministic computation produces the same observable result for the same inputs and relevant environment. Random seeds can help reproduce pseudo-random sequences, but do not control clocks, thread scheduling, filesystem ordering or changing external services.

### Focused example
~~~python
import random
first = random.Random(17).sample(range(100), 5)
second = random.Random(17).sample(range(100), 5)
assert first == second
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
Remove the explicit seed and observe possible variation, then sort an unordered collection before comparing output. For tests with dates, inject a fixed clock instead of depending on the current time. Explain which dependencies still prevent complete reproducibility.

**Reference:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/random.html

## Dictionary

### Concept in practice
A dictionary associates unique keys with values and typically supports efficient lookup by key. In Python, keys must be hashable, and assigning to an existing key replaces its value. Lookup performance is usually good on average but not a contractual constant-time guarantee in all circumstances.

### Focused example
~~~python
totals = {}
for name in ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Ada']:
    totals[name] = totals.get(name, 0) + 1
assert totals == {'Ada': 2, 'Grace': 1}
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
Try using a list as a dictionary key and record the resulting TypeError. Compare `d.get(k)` with `d[k]` when a key is absent; distinguish legitimate missing data from a default zero.

**Reference:** https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#dictionaries

## Dynamic typing

### Concept in practice
In dynamically typed languages such as Python, values carry types and names may refer to different types over time. This is not the same as having no type rules; incorrect operations still raise errors at runtime. Optional static annotations can help tooling without converting Python into a statically enforced runtime.

### Focused example
~~~python
value = 3
value = 'three'
assert isinstance(value, str)
try:
    _ = value + 1
except TypeError: pass
else: raise AssertionError('expected a type error')
~~~

### Exercise and common pitfall
Design a function accepting unknown JSON and validate with isinstance before arithmetic. Compare its runtime behavior with a type-checker warning on `value + 1`; avoid treating type hints as automatic input validation.

**Reference:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html

## Encapsulation

### Meaning and constraints
Encapsulation places state and the operations that preserve its rules behind a deliberate interface. Python's leading underscore is a convention, not hard access control. Clients should call methods that preserve an invariant rather than mutating internal fields directly.

### A concrete use
~~~python
class Balance:
    def __init__(self): self._cents = 0
    def add(self, cents):
        if type(cents) is not int or cents < 0: raise ValueError('invalid amount')
        self._cents += cents
    @property
    def cents(self): return self._cents
b = Balance(); b.add(25); assert b.cents == 25
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Try add(-1) and add(True). Explain why direct assignment to `_cents` is still technically possible, so an API boundary must also enforce caller privileges where relevant.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/classes.html#private-variables


### Glossary: encoding, exceptions and expressions

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1100.html

# Glossary: encoding, exceptions and expressions

## Encoding

### Meaning and constraints
An encoding maps characters to bytes and back. UTF-8 represents the same Unicode text with a variable number of bytes per code point. Decoding arbitrary bytes with the wrong encoding fails or corrupts text; a byte offset is not the same as a character index.

### A concrete use
~~~python
text = 'Γεια'
data = text.encode('utf-8')
assert data.decode('utf-8') == text
assert len(data) > len(text)
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Write the bytes to a scratch binary file and test decode with utf-8. Introduce invalid UTF-8 byte `b'\xff'` and catch UnicodeDecodeError. Do not use errors='ignore' to hide data loss.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/howto/unicode.html

## Exception

### Meaning and constraints
An exception reports an abnormal condition and transfers control to a matching handler. Catching a specific error close to the boundary lets expected failures be handled while unexpected programming defects remain visible. Catching every exception and returning success conceals faults.

### A concrete use
~~~python
def port(text):
    try: number = int(text)
    except ValueError as exc: raise ValueError('port must be decimal') from exc
    if not 1 <= number <= 65535: raise ValueError('port out of range')
    return number
assert port('443') == 443
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Test 'abc', '0' and '65536' separately. Trace where exceptions are raised versus caught and preserve original cause using `raise ... from ...` when translating an error between layers.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/errors.html

## Expression

### Meaning and constraints
An expression evaluates to a value; a statement performs an action in the language grammar. Operators, precedence and side effects affect the value produced. Parentheses clarify intent even when precedence rules would produce the same result.

### A concrete use
~~~python
a, b, c = 2, 3, 4
assert a + b * c == 14
assert (a + b) * c == 20
square = lambda n: n * n
assert square(a + 1) == 9
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Write the syntax tree for `2+3*4` and `(2+3)*4`. Distinguish `n = 5` (assignment statement) from `n == 5` (comparison expression) in Python, then predict the result before running.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html

## File descriptor

### Meaning and constraints
On POSIX-like systems a file descriptor is a small integer handle that a process uses for an open file, pipe or socket. Standard input, output and error commonly occupy descriptors 0, 1 and 2. A descriptor refers to an open resource, not directly to a filename.

### A concrete use
~~~python
import os
read_fd, write_fd = os.pipe()
try:
    os.write(write_fd, b'ok')
    assert os.read(read_fd, 2) == b'ok'
finally:
    os.close(read_fd); os.close(write_fd)
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Explain why both pipe ends must be closed on failure and success. Investigate what happens if a long-lived process leaks descriptors. POSIX descriptor APIs may differ on Windows; this example requires os.pipe support.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#file-descriptor-operations

## Finite state machine

### Meaning and constraints
A finite-state machine models a system using a limited set of states and explicitly permitted transitions. Rather than scattering booleans such as is_loading/is_done/is_error that can contradict one another, an enum makes mutually exclusive states representable.

### A concrete use
~~~python
from enum import Enum
class Status(Enum): IDLE=1; LOADING=2; DONE=3
allowed = {Status.IDLE:{Status.LOADING}, Status.LOADING:{Status.DONE}, Status.DONE:set()}
assert Status.DONE in allowed[Status.LOADING]
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Design a retry transition DONE→LOADING only if your product genuinely permits it. Test an invalid direct IDLE→DONE jump and explain which code layer must reject it.

**Further reading:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite-state_machine


### Environment variable

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1101.html

# Environment variable — explicit process configuration, not secret storage

## Precise meaning
An environment variable is a named string in the process environment. Child processes normally inherit a copy of the parent's environment at launch, unless the launcher supplies a different one. It is useful for application mode, executable search paths and nonsecret configuration. It is **not** a secure password vault: diagnostic tools, logs, debug reports, other permitted processes or accidentally printed subprocess commands can reveal secrets stored there.

## Deterministic Python 3 lab
Save as environment_lab.py and run python3 environment_lab.py. This test passes a dedicated environment mapping to subprocess rather than mutating global configuration. It proves the child sees a selected mode, missing configuration has a deliberate default, invalid modes fail and child changes do not flow back into the parent.

~~~python
import os
import subprocess
import sys

KEY = 'DEDSEC_DEMO_MODE'
ALLOWED = {'development', 'test', 'production'}

def read_mode(environment):
    value = environment.get(KEY, 'development')
    if value not in ALLOWED:
        raise ValueError('unexpected mode')
    return value

def run_child(value):
    env = dict(os.environ)
    env.pop(KEY, None)
    if value is not None:
        env[KEY] = value
    command = [sys.executable, '-c',
               'import os; print(os.environ.get("DEDSEC_DEMO_MODE", "unset"))']
    return subprocess.check_output(command, env=env, text=True).strip()

assert read_mode({}) == 'development'
assert read_mode({KEY: 'test'}) == 'test'
try:
    read_mode({KEY: 'unknown'})
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError('unknown mode was accepted')
assert run_child('test') == 'test'
assert run_child(None) == 'unset'
original = os.environ.get(KEY)
command = [sys.executable, '-c',
           'import os; os.environ["DEDSEC_DEMO_MODE"]="child"; print(os.environ["DEDSEC_DEMO_MODE"])']
assert subprocess.check_output(command, text=True).strip() == 'child'
assert os.environ.get(KEY) == original
print('PASS environment: injection, defaults, validation, parent isolation')
~~~

## Understand the lifetime and trust boundary
The subprocess env argument controls what the newly launched process receives. Altering os.environ in the Python parent affects later children it launches but not a shell that launched Python earlier. Modifying the environment inside a child does not rewrite its parent environment. APP_MODE-style flags must be validated just like file inputs: accepting arbitrary modes can enable unsafe debugging, silent feature switches or surprising output. If a key holds confidential credentials, use an appropriate secrets provider or a protected credential mechanism and never log its value. This example uses only a fake nonsecret mode value.

## Experiments and diagnostics
1. Launch the script with its demo mode absent and set to test. Show the difference between a child's supplied environment mapping and the inherited parent mapping.
2. Print a stable allowlisted diagnostic such as whether a key is present, never its sensitive value. Explain what a crash report could expose.
3. Try unsupported mode staging. Confirm failure occurs before starting work and that user-provided mode text is not trusted automatically.
4. Compare behavior on Linux/Termux and Windows, including process launch conventions and platform-specific case handling of environment names.

**Evidence:** PASS, a parent/child state table, one invalid-mode failure and a stated policy for protecting credentials.


### Glossary: functions, garbage collection and generics

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1106.html

# Glossary: functions, garbage collection and generics

## Function

### Meaning and constraints
A function packages a repeatable computation behind inputs and a return value. A good contract identifies accepted types, invalid inputs, side effects and guarantees. Calling a function does not imply it is pure: it may modify files, global state or a database.

### A concrete use
~~~python
def area(width: float, height: float) -> float:
    if width < 0 or height < 0: raise ValueError('negative dimension')
    return width * height
assert area(3, 4) == 12
assert area(0, 5) == 0
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Add tests for a negative dimension and a nonnumeric input. Decide whether a function annotated with float should validate runtime types at an external boundary; annotations alone do not enforce conversion.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#defining-functions

## Garbage collection

### Meaning and constraints
Garbage collection reclaims memory for unreachable objects according to runtime rules. Python primarily uses reference counting with a cyclic collector, while other runtimes may use tracing collectors. Collection frees memory resources, but does not guarantee prompt release of file handles or locks.

### A concrete use
~~~python
from contextlib import closing
from io import StringIO
with closing(StringIO('test')) as stream:
    assert stream.read() == 'test'
assert stream.closed
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Explain why an explicit context manager is preferable for file handles. Sketch a two-object reference cycle and note that memory collection timing is not a portable API contract.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/gc.html

## Generic type

### Meaning and constraints
A generic type is parameterized by another type so one abstraction can preserve information about several concrete kinds of data. In Python, `list[int]` communicates element expectations to type checkers, but does not reject wrong elements at runtime by itself.

### A concrete use
~~~python
from typing import TypeVar
T = TypeVar('T')
def first(items: list[T]) -> T | None:
    return items[0] if items else None
assert first([3,4]) == 3
assert first([]) is None
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Ask a type checker to infer the return type for list[str] and list[int]. Compare the compile-time checking with a runtime validator that must still inspect unknown JSON elements.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html

## Git

### Meaning and constraints
Git is a distributed version-control system: a local clone usually has commits, branches and metadata independently of the remote server. `fetch` updates knowledge of remote refs, `merge` or `rebase` reconciles histories, and `push` publishes local commits if permitted.

### A concrete use
~~~sh
git status --short --branch
git log --oneline -5
git remote -v
git fetch origin
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Use a disposable clone to compare `git status` before and after `fetch`. Confirm that fetch alone does not alter tracked working files. Do not force-push or reset production branches to compensate for confusion.

**Further reading:** https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Getting-Started-What-is-Git%3F

## Hash function

### Meaning and constraints
A hash function deterministically maps input bytes to a fixed-size digest. Cryptographic SHA-256 aims to make accidental and deliberate collision construction impractical, but a digest only checks equality relative to a trusted known value. A dictionary's internal hash has different security goals.

### A concrete use
~~~python
import hashlib
h = lambda b: hashlib.sha256(b).hexdigest()
assert h(b'abc') == 'ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad'
assert h(b'abc') != h(b'abd')
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Hash a file before and after changing one byte; record both digests. Explain why publishing a malicious binary and its matching digest on the same compromised page offers no identity guarantee.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html


### Glossary: heaps, HTTP and idempotence

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1111.html

# Glossary: heaps, HTTP and idempotence

## Heap

### Meaning and constraints
The word heap has two separate uses: the dynamic memory region used for allocations, and a priority-queue data structure. A binary min-heap stores a partial ordering that makes the smallest key accessible efficiently; it does not keep every element globally sorted.

### A concrete use
~~~python
import heapq
items = [9, 2, 5, 1]
heapq.heapify(items)
assert heapq.heappop(items) == 1
assert heapq.heappop(items) == 2
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Print the internal heap list after heapify and prove it need not be sorted. Distinguish the O(log n) push/pop operations from a memory allocation on the process heap.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html

## HTTP

### Meaning and constraints
HTTP defines a client-server exchange of methods, target resources, headers, status codes and possibly bodies. HTTP is stateless at the protocol layer; applications can correlate requests using cookies, tokens and server-side sessions. A 200 status does not certify that JSON data has the right schema.

### A concrete use
~~~http
GET /status HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"ok":true}
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Sketch separate responses 200, 404, 429 and 503. Describe which failures can be retried, when Retry-After matters, and why CORS is a browser enforcement mechanism rather than an HTTP authentication system.

**Further reading:** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Overview

## Idempotence

### Meaning and constraints
An operation is idempotent when repeating it has the same intended effect as doing it once. Setting a flag to true is idempotent, whereas incrementing a counter ordinarily is not. In HTTP, method idempotence is about intended server effects, not necessarily identical response bytes.

### A concrete use
~~~python
state = {'enabled': False, 'counter': 0}
def enable(): state['enabled'] = True
def increment(): state['counter'] += 1
enable(); enable(); assert state['enabled'] is True
increment(); increment(); assert state['counter'] == 2
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Design an API endpoint that accepts an idempotency key for a payment-like test action. Model a repeated request after a network timeout and prevent accidental duplicate writes; don't use real payment services.

**Further reading:** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Idempotent

## Immutable

### Meaning and constraints
An immutable value cannot be changed in place through its exposed interface. Python tuples are immutable containers but may contain references to mutable objects; immutability of the outer tuple does not recursively freeze everything it contains.

### A concrete use
~~~python
items = ([1,2],)
items[0].append(3)
assert items == ([1,2,3],)
# items[0] = [4]  # TypeError: tuple assignment is forbidden
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Compare a frozen dataclass with a regular one, then test a frozen field that holds a list. Decide when a deep immutable representation is needed for safe caching or cross-thread messaging.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#tuples

## Index

### Meaning and constraints
An index can be a position into an ordered collection or a separate data structure accelerating database lookups. Python sequence indexes usually start at zero and negative indexes count from the end; a database index instead stores searchable keys and references to records.

### A concrete use
~~~python
words = ['first', 'second', 'third']
assert words[0] == 'first'
assert words[-1] == 'third'
assert words[1:3] == ['second', 'third']
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Try words[3] and record IndexError. Then create an indexed SQLite column and compare EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN before and after, noting that an optimizer may avoid an index for a tiny table.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#common-sequence-operations


### Glossary: injection, interfaces and interpreters

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1116.html

# Glossary: injection, interfaces and interpreters

## Injection

### Meaning and constraints
Injection occurs when untrusted data is interpreted as commands or executable syntax instead of remaining data. SQL string concatenation, shell execution and unsafe HTML construction cross different trust boundaries; escaping for one context does not protect another.

### A concrete use
~~~python
import sqlite3
c = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
c.execute('CREATE TABLE users(name TEXT)')
c.execute('INSERT INTO users VALUES (?)', ('Ada',))
assert c.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE name=?', ("' OR 1=1 --",)).fetchall() == []
c.close()
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Compare parameterized SQL with a string concatenation example *only in a disposable local database*. Explain why identifiers still require an allowlist and why subprocess arguments should be passed as arrays with shell=False.

**Further reading:** https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html

## Interface

### Meaning and constraints
An interface describes the operations available to a caller without requiring them to know the implementation. A useful contract specifies accepted inputs, return values, errors and side effects. Two implementations that share method names are not necessarily behaviorally substitutable.

### A concrete use
~~~python
from typing import Protocol
class Store(Protocol):
    def get(self, key: str) -> str | None: ...
class MemoryStore:
    def __init__(self): self.data = {'x':'ok'}
    def get(self, key): return self.data.get(key)
assert MemoryStore().get('x') == 'ok'
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Build a second Store that reads from a scratch file and ensure both use the same missing-key behavior. Note that Protocol checks by static type tools do not perform full runtime schema validation.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Protocol

## Interpreter

### Meaning and constraints
An interpreter executes a language's program or intermediate representation, often evaluating statements as it runs. CPython compiles Python source to bytecode before its virtual machine executes it; therefore 'interpreted' does not mean source always runs without compilation.

### A concrete use
~~~python
import dis
def add(a, b): return a + b
assert add(2,3) == 5
dis.dis(add)  # shows bytecode for the current interpreter
~~~

### Challenge and misconception
Compare `python -m py_compile example.py` with running the script. Observe that syntax compilation can succeed even when a runtime branch contains a division by zero. Don't treat disassembly as portable across Python versions.

**Further reading:** https://docs.python.org/3/library/dis.html

## Invariant

### Definition and boundaries
A property preserved after each allowed operation. If a debit is permitted only when the balance can cover it, balance >= 0 remains true. An invariant is stronger than a check performed only once.

### Working miniature
~~~text
def debit(balance, amount):
    if not 0 <= amount <= balance: raise ValueError('bad debit')
    return balance-amount
assert debit(10,3)==7
~~~

### Guided investigation
Try 0, 10 and 11 as withdrawals from 10. Prove every valid operation preserves a nonnegative result, and make sure the invalid call raises.

### Demonstrate the invariant, not just a passing output
In prefix sums the claim before iteration i is that total equals the sum of elements before i. Initialization uses zero; the next addition preserves that claim; termination proves all elements were included.

~~~python
def prefix(items):
    total, result = 0, []
    for i, value in enumerate(items):
        assert total == sum(items[:i])
        total += value
        result.append(total)
    return result
assert prefix([2,-1,4]) == [2,1,5]
assert prefix([]) == []
~~~

Move the assertion after the update and observe the first failing case. Remember that Python assertions can be disabled in optimized execution and cannot replace input validation.


### Glossary: JSON, lazy evaluation and linters

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1120.html

# Glossary: JSON, lazy evaluation and linters

## JSON

### Definition and boundaries
A standard text encoding for objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. JSON syntax is not JavaScript object-literal syntax: comments and trailing commas are invalid. A parser verifies grammar rather than the application's schema.

### Working miniature
~~~text
import json
d=json.loads('{"active":true,"count":3}')
assert d['active'] is True
assert type(d['count']) is int
~~~

### Guided investigation
Test duplicate keys, a top-level list and an unknown field. Add separate schema validation that checks exact keys; default json.loads normally retains the last duplicated key.

## Lazy evaluation

### Definition and boundaries
Computation deferred until a result is demanded. Python generators yield incrementally, while Haskell uses non-strict evaluation more broadly. Delayed work changes when errors and side effects occur.

### Working miniature
~~~text
def numbers():
    yield 2
    yield 4
it=numbers()
assert next(it)==2
assert list(it)==[4]
~~~

### Guided investigation
Add a print before the first yield. Confirm it does not run at generator creation and that the iterator is exhausted after consumption.

### Check your understanding
For Lazy evaluation, change one input in the example and explain whether the observed behavior still satisfies the stated definition. Record the exact output and distinguish a program error from a mistaken assumption.

## Linter

### Definition and boundaries
Tool that checks source code against configurable static rules. It may find unused imports and suspicious constructs without executing the application; this does not replace behavioral testing or type checking.

### Working miniature
~~~text
def ratio(total, used):
    if total <= 0: raise ValueError('invalid total')
    return used/total
assert ratio(4,2)==0.5
~~~

### Guided investigation
Insert an unused variable into a scratch file, run a suitable linter and remove it without changing the validation. Compare warning output with an actual failing unit test.

## List

### Definition and boundaries
Ordered collection preserving element positions. Python's list is a mutable dynamic array with fast indexing; inserting at the beginning can shift the rest of the elements. Other languages may implement linked lists differently.

### Working miniature
~~~text
names=['Ada','Grace']; names.append('Lin')
assert names[-1]=='Lin'
assert names[1:]==['Grace','Lin']
~~~

### Guided investigation
Compare append with insert(0, item) for a longer list. Copy a nested list shallowly, modify an inner list and observe shared references.

## Lock

### Definition and boundaries
Synchronization primitive guarding a critical section against concurrent mutation. A lock protects only the operations that consistently acquire it; it cannot automatically protect external state or turn multiple SQL statements into a transaction.

### Working miniature
~~~text
from threading import Lock
lock=Lock(); count=[0]
with lock: count[0]+=1
assert count==[1]
~~~

### Guided investigation
Run concurrent increments using the same lock. Then sketch how two threads acquiring locks A/B in opposite orders can deadlock.

### Four competing threads and one protected section
A lock protects a read-modify-write operation among cooperating threads. It guarantees exclusion, not scheduling order.

~~~python
from threading import Thread, Lock
mutex, counter = Lock(), [0]
def run():
    for _ in range(1000):
        with mutex:
            counter[0] += 1
jobs = [Thread(target=run) for _ in range(4)]
for t in jobs: t.start()
for t in jobs: t.join()
assert counter[0] == 4000
~~~

Extend the experiment with a count of workers currently inside the protected section; maximum concurrency there must be one. A standard Lock is not reentrant; acquiring it twice from one thread can deadlock. Do not hold the lock while awaiting network services.


### Glossary: logging, leaks and schema migrations

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1125.html

# Glossary: logging, leaks and schema migrations

## Logging

### Definition and boundaries
Recording contextual events with severity levels, timestamps and correlation IDs for diagnosis. Logs are observable output that can leak tokens or personal data if unsanitized.

### Working miniature
~~~text
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logging.info('processed %d records',3)
~~~

### Guided investigation
Log a rejected record with a synthetic request ID while deliberately omitting credentials. Check which fields reach the handler, not only the console text.

### Check your understanding
For Logging, change one input in the example and explain whether the observed behavior still satisfies the stated definition. Record the exact output and distinguish a program error from a mistaken assumption.

## Memory leak

### Definition and boundaries
Unexpected retention of objects past their useful lifetime. Long-lived caches, callbacks or references can cause this even with a garbage collector. High memory use from legitimate data is not necessarily a leak.

### Working miniature
~~~text
from collections import deque
recent=deque(maxlen=10)
for n in range(10000): recent.append(n)
assert len(recent)==10
~~~

### Guided investigation
Compare an unbounded list with this bounded deque under repeated inputs. Use tracemalloc snapshots to identify retained allocations instead of guessing.

### Retained references make objects live longer
An object may remain reachable through a growing registry even when its original local variable is deleted. Use a weak reference to observe this without exhausting memory.

~~~python
import gc, weakref
class Entry: pass
registry = []
entry = Entry()
watch = weakref.ref(entry)
registry.append(entry)
del entry
gc.collect()
assert watch() is not None
registry.clear()
gc.collect()
assert watch() is None
~~~

Design a cache with a 100-entry maximum, then compare object retention after thousands of unique keys. Resident-set size alone is not sufficient to prove a leak because allocators may keep free pools; inspect surviving objects and owners.

## Migration

### Definition and boundaries
A controlled upgrade from one data schema or service version to another. Migrations must consider existing rows, partial deployment and rollback options rather than editing a schema once.

### Working miniature
~~~text
CREATE TABLE tasks(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,title TEXT);
ALTER TABLE tasks ADD COLUMN archived INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;
~~~

### Guided investigation
Use a disposable SQLite database containing older rows; verify that the new archived field is 0 and plan how a rollback would handle it.

### Upgrade old rows without losing their values
A schema migration is successful only if existing records remain valid and the new schema is compatible with the application.

~~~python
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE tasks(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,title TEXT)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO tasks(title) VALUES (?)", ("review",))
with db:
    db.execute("ALTER TABLE tasks ADD COLUMN archived INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0")
assert db.execute("SELECT title,archived FROM tasks").fetchone() == ("review",0)
db.close()
~~~

Extend the lab with PRAGMA user_version and execute the upgrade twice. The second pass should detect that the new version is already installed. For destructive migrations, plan backups and rollback before applying changes; DDL transaction semantics vary across engines.

### Glossary: optionals, overflow and package managers

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1133.html

# Glossary: optionals, overflow and package managers

## Optional

### Precise meaning
An API that represents present and absent results as distinct cases. Rust Option<T>, TypeScript optional properties and Python's T|None annotation describe related concepts but have different runtime behavior.

### Reference experiment
~~~text
def first(items: list[int]) -> int | None:
    return items[0] if items else None
assert first([]) is None
assert first([0])==0
~~~

### Investigate the boundary
Replace None with an explicit found/missing tagged result and compare caller behavior when the valid result is zero.

### Zero is a value, not a missing argument
Represent absent data explicitly. Using a truthiness test merges zero with None and may create subtle application errors.

~~~python
def remaining(capacity, limit=None):
    if capacity < 0 or (limit is not None and limit < 0):
        raise ValueError("negative")
    return capacity if limit is None else min(capacity, limit)
assert remaining(7) == 7
assert remaining(7, 0) == 0
assert remaining(7, 3) == 3
~~~

Deliberately replace the None test with a falsy-value test and reproduce the zero-limit bug. A tagged Result is more expressive if missing, invalid and present are distinct outcomes. Static Optional annotations do not validate untrusted JSON at runtime.

## Overflow

### Precise meaning
Numeric result outside a fixed type's range. Languages can trap, wrap or reject overflow. Python's arbitrary-precision integers are different from unsigned 8-bit registers.

### Reference experiment
~~~text
def add_u8(a,b):
    if not (0<=a<=255 and 0<=b<=255): raise ValueError()
    if a > 255-b: raise OverflowError()
    return a+b
assert add_u8(255,0)==255
~~~

### Investigate the boundary
Try add_u8(250,6) and compare its error with an intentionally wrapping 8-bit counter. Explain why overflow is dangerous in money calculations.

### Check fixed-width limits before serializing
Python integers are arbitrary precision, but a binary unsigned byte has a maximum of 255. Validation must respect the destination type.

~~~python
def add_u8(a, b):
    if any(type(v) is not int or not 0 <= v <= 255 for v in (a,b)):
        raise ValueError("unsigned byte expected")
    if a > 255-b:
        raise OverflowError("byte overflow")
    return a+b
assert add_u8(200, 55) == 255
try:
    add_u8(200, 56)
except OverflowError: pass
else: raise AssertionError("invalid result accepted")
~~~

Contrast rejection with wrapping modulo 256. Wrapping may be correct for some protocols but dangerous for sizes and financial balances. C signed integer overflow is undefined behavior rather than guaranteed wraparound.

## Package manager

### Precise meaning
A dependency resolver and installer whose trust boundary includes registries, lockfiles, version constraints, installation hooks and platform compatibility.

### Reference experiment
~~~text
python -m pip --version
python -m pip list --format=columns
~~~

### Investigate the boundary
In a disposable virtual environment install a trusted pinned package, inspect its exact resolved version and compare to an unpinned requirement.

### Independent check
For Package manager, document the expected outcome before running the sample. Change one important assumption and decide whether the failure belongs to the caller, the implementation or the environment.

### Pointer

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1139.html

# Pointer — bounds, aliasing and the lifetime contract

## Exact meaning
A pointer identifies a location or object in an address space; it is not a guarantee that the object remains alive, belongs to the right type or contains the required number of elements. In C a valid pointer can refer to the first element of an array, to one of its interior elements or one position past its end. The one-past pointer may be formed in limited circumstances but must not be dereferenced. Accessing released storage, a dead stack object or an out-of-bounds element has undefined behavior.

## Runnable C11 example
Save as pointer.c. Compile with gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pedantic -fsanitize=address,undefined pointer.c -o pointer when the sanitizer runtime is available, then execute ./pointer. The code deliberately avoids constructing an invalid access; assertions establish observable aliasing and rejection of invalid indices.

~~~c
#include <assert.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdio.h>

static bool replace_at(int *data, size_t length, size_t index, int value) {
    if (data == NULL || index >= length) return false;
    data[index] = value;
    return true;
}
int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {3, 5, 8};
    size_t count = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
    int *second = &numbers[1];
    assert(*second == 5);
    assert(replace_at(numbers, count, 1, 9));
    assert(*second == 9);
    assert(!replace_at(numbers, count, count, 10));
    assert(numbers[2] == 8);
    assert(!replace_at(NULL, 0, 0, 1));
    puts("PASS pointer: alias, lifetime-safe scope, bounds, NULL");
}
~~~

## Reason about the memory model
The variable second points to numbers[1], so replacing that element changes the value seen through both expressions. It remains valid only while numbers exists in the same call frame. The length parameter is an independent contract: a pointer value cannot reveal the array length in a called C function. C does not automatically check pointer bounds. Passing NULL is rejected here before dereference, but non-NULL does not prove an address is valid. A helper returning &local_variable from a function would violate lifetime even if its printed address looks plausible.

## Controlled investigations
1. Change the index to count and verify replacement fails without modifying any item. Explain why writing numbers[count] would be undefined rather than a legitimate boundary test.
2. Move the array into a helper, return a pointer to a local variable and explain the failure **without executing** the invalid dereference. Compare with storage owned by the caller.
3. Separate pointer constness: contrast const int * (read-only through the pointer) and int *const (nonreassignable pointer variable).
4. Compile in debug and optimized builds; use AddressSanitizer only for deliberately isolated synthetic tests. Never infer safety solely from an absence of crashes.

**Evidence:** the PASS line, compiler command/version, correct array size and an explicit lifetime/ownership statement.

## Promise

### Precise meaning

async function answer(){ return 42; }

### Precise meaning
An agreement specifying message format, sequencing, error responses and roles between communicating components. HTTP is a protocol; JSON alone is just one representation.

### Reference experiment

GET /status HTTP/1.1

# Expected success might be HTTP/1.1 200 OK
~~~

## Race condition

### Precise meaning
Behavior that changes when independent operations interleave in different orders. A race condition may be logical even without unsynchronized memory access.

### Reference experiment
~~~text
balance=10
# Two workers both read 10, calculate 3 and 4 debit independently.
# Last write wins: incorrect final balance instead of 3.
~~~

Model two concurrent debits as a timeline, identify the read-modify-write race and fix it with a transaction or suitable synchronization.

## Recursion

### Precise meaning
A function calling itself on a smaller subproblem. Correct recursion needs a base case and a measure that moves toward it; otherwise stack depth can grow without bound.

### Reference experiment
~~~text
def factorial(n):
    if n < 0: raise ValueError()
    if n == 0: return 1
    return n*factorial(n-1)
assert factorial(4)==24
~~~

### Investigate the boundary
Trace the call frames for factorial(3), including return order. Compare with an iterative version for large n and test invalid negatives.

### Independent check
For Recursion, document the expected outcome before running the sample. Change one important assumption and decide whether the failure belongs to the caller, the implementation or the environment.

## Refactoring

### Precise meaning
Change to internal structure while preserving externally observable behavior under a defined contract. Tests and behavior checks provide evidence; renaming alone is not sufficient validation.

### Reference experiment
~~~text
def total(items):
    return sum(items)
assert total([2,3])==5
~~~

### Investigate the boundary
Extract a long conditional into a named function and run identical positive, empty and invalid inputs before/after. Compare outputs and exceptions.

### Independent check
For Refactoring, document the expected outcome before running the sample. Change one important assumption and decide whether the failure belongs to the caller, the implementation or the environment.

## Regression test

A test retaining a demonstrated bug's reproduction so that future edits detect its return. A regression test should fail on the defective version and pass on the corrected one.

## Schema

### Actual meaning
A specification of allowed fields, types and constraints. Parsing JSON only guarantees syntax; a schema can require nonempty names, reject unknown keys or specify migration compatibility.

def check(row):

Turning in-memory values into a transferable or storable representation. Deserialization reverses that transformation, but not all object types round-trip without information loss.

### Sandbox

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1150.html

# Sandbox — separate a working folder from a security boundary

## What this term means
A sandbox restricts what a process can observe or modify, usually by constraining system calls, filesystem access, credentials, namespaces, permissions or network routes. A temporary folder, Python virtual environment, Git branch and browser private window are **not** by themselves security sandboxes for hostile programs.

## Safe contrast: scratch directory, not isolation
~~~python
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as root:
    workspace = Path(root)
    file = workspace / "sample.txt"
    file.write_text("training data", encoding="utf-8")
    assert file.read_text(encoding="utf-8") == "training data"
~~~
This snippet organizes disposable **trusted** work. It does not prevent the same Python process from reading other paths accessible to its OS user. Do not execute unknown binaries or unreviewed scripts inside it and assume safety.

## Design a real boundary
For an offline lesson viewer, the safe default is *render inert lesson text*. If code must be executed, prefer a separately provisioned operating-system sandbox or VM, restrict writable mounts, block network egress where not required, use an unprivileged identity, set CPU/time/memory limits and provide no credentials. The exact controls depend on Android/Termux versus desktop Linux versus Windows. A phone app's Android sandbox is not equivalent to rootless Linux namespaces.

## Adversarial verification
1. Make a permissions table: lesson reader can read packaged lessons but cannot write outside an approved scratch area.
2. Attempt a harmless write into a deliberately protected test directory **inside a disposable test environment** and expect a denied operation.
3. Confirm the sandbox cannot reach an example local service when network access is disabled. Do not probe systems you do not own.
4. Confirm that timeout/cancellation stops runaway work, and document what happens to children.
5. Review whether diagnostic logs or exceptions expose secrets from the host.

## Evidence
List the real isolation mechanism, OS version, mount/network privileges and both positive and denied tests. If you only used TemporaryDirectory, describe it as cleanup, not isolation.


### Side effect

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1153.html

# Side effect — separate decisions from observable changes

## Precise meaning
A side effect is a change observable outside a function's returned value: a file write, network request, log line, mutation of a shared object or system clock dependency. Pure calculations are easier to reproduce because their result depends only on their explicit arguments. Separating calculation from a side-effectful boundary lets tests inject a writer and verify failure without writing real files or relying on personal data.

## Runnable Python 3 lab
Save as side_lab.py and run python3 side_lab.py. A pure compute function produces integer-cent totals; render produces a deterministic JSON string. The publish function invokes a caller-supplied writer only after validation and rendering succeed. The test simulates both a bad input and a write failure.

~~~python
import json

def compute(entries):
    totals = {}
    for category, cents in entries:
        if not isinstance(category, str) or not category or type(cents) is not int or cents < 0:
            raise ValueError('invalid entry')
        totals[category] = totals.get(category, 0) + cents
    return totals

def render(entries):
    return json.dumps(compute(entries), ensure_ascii=False, sort_keys=True) + '\n'

def publish(entries, writer):
    payload = render(entries)  # Validate before invoking any side-effectful function.
    writer(payload)

out = []
publish([('βιβλία', 120), ('books', 30)], out.append)
assert out == ['{"books": 30, "βιβλία": 120}\n']
try:
    publish([('valid', 10), ('invalid', -1)], out.append)
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError('invalid input published')
assert len(out) == 1
try:
    publish([('books', 1)], lambda x: (_ for _ in ()).throw(OSError('disk unavailable')))
except OSError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError('write failure hidden')
assert render([('βιβλία', 120), ('books', 30)]) == out[0]
print('PASS side effects: pure core, injected writer, errors')
~~~

## What the test does and does not guarantee
The first call appends one string to a test list, with Unicode category names preserved and keys sorted. Invalid input fails before the writer is invoked, leaving the list unchanged. A writer can still fail after partially writing bytes; this simple abstraction cannot guarantee atomic filesystem updates. For an actual report, use a temporary file, write and close it successfully, then replace the destination where atomic rename is supported. The pure compute function avoids modifying its input and uses integer cents rather than floating-point money.

## Targeted exercises
1. Add a shared global counter to compute and run the same test twice. Explain which purity guarantee was violated.
2. Inject a writer that records only the first three bytes before raising OSError. Decide which layer must implement atomic replacement.
3. Add a category containing a comma or Greek text; verify UTF-8 rendering and deterministic sorting without real I/O.
4. Test a negative count and a boolean masquerading as an integer. Show that the writer receives no content after a validation failure.

**Evidence:** PASS output, one stable JSON record, a failed-input test that leaves state intact and a documented limitation of partial writer failures.


### SQL parameterization — glossary definition

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1154.html

# SQL parameterization — data stays data

## The trust boundary
A SQL parameter placeholder represents a **value**, not executable query syntax. Binding values prevents user text from changing SQL structure, but it does not validate business rules or grant database permissions. Table names and ORDER BY column identifiers require explicit allowlists; placeholders cannot safely stand in for arbitrary identifiers.

## Runnable sqlite3 exercise
~~~python
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE inventory (sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY, qty INTEGER)")
db.executemany(
    "INSERT INTO inventory(sku, qty) VALUES (?, ?)",
    [("bolt", 4), ("nut", 2)],
)
input_sku = "bolt' OR 1=1 --"
found = db.execute(
    "SELECT qty FROM inventory WHERE sku = ?", (input_sku,)
).fetchall()
assert found == []
valid = db.execute(
    "SELECT qty FROM inventory WHERE sku = ?", ("bolt",)
).fetchone()
assert valid == (4,)
db.close()
~~~
A parameter is transmitted as a value; the apostrophe in the malicious-looking string cannot create an OR clause. The negative test returns no matching SKU. Dynamic SQL created by string concatenation would not have this separation.

## Deeper checks
1. Use a positive test with a quote inside a legitimate SKU. Query it exactly with a bound value.
2. Try replacing the table name using a placeholder and record the syntax error. Choose a table name from a fixed, reviewed mapping instead.
3. For a user-selected sort order, map a symbolic option to a known literal SQL fragment; do not concatenate raw user input.
4. Test invalid quantities separately: parameterization does not reject -5 unless a CHECK constraint or application validation requires it.
5. Wrap multiple writes in a transaction and test a deliberate constraint violation. Confirm the database state after rollback.

## Acceptance and limits
Run the assertions in a temporary in-memory SQLite database, review the query text and check that no user value is concatenated into SQL. Other database drivers use different placeholder syntax. Parameterization does not replace authorization or least-privilege database accounts.


### Glossary: stacks, static typing and streams

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/en-1155.html

# Glossary: stacks, static typing and streams

## Stack

### Actual meaning
Last-in-first-out structure: push adds an item and pop removes the most recently added one. Program call stacks also hold execution frames, but they are not the same as an explicit data-structure stack.

### Concrete starting point
~~~text
stack=[]
stack.append('open'); stack.append('close')
assert stack.pop()=='close'
assert stack.pop()=='open'
~~~

### Apply the rule
Use a stack to validate matching parentheses, then test an unexpected closing bracket and a remaining opening bracket.

### Diagnose a counterexample
For Stack, write down the expected outcome, deliberately break an assumption from this specific example, and determine what must be checked at the boundary before this behavior could be reused safely.

## Static typing

### Actual meaning
Checking types before program execution or during compilation, as in TypeScript and Rust. Static type guarantees depend on language soundness and do not automatically validate external JSON at runtime.

### Concrete starting point
~~~text
type Record = {score: number};
const r: Record = {score: 3};
// const bad: Record = {score: '3'}; // compile error
~~~

### Apply the rule
Compile with strict mode, introduce the bad assignment, then demonstrate a runtime parser that rejects unexpected string data.

### Diagnose a counterexample
For Static typing, write down the expected outcome, deliberately break an assumption from this specific example, and determine what must be checked at the boundary before this behavior could be reused safely.

## Stream

### Actual meaning
Sequence processed incrementally rather than necessarily stored all at once. File streams, network streams and async iterators differ in buffering, backpressure and error reporting.

### Concrete starting point
~~~text
from io import StringIO
with StringIO('first\nsecond\n') as src:
    assert [line.strip() for line in src]==['first','second']
~~~

### Apply the rule
Process a large synthetic file line by line without readlines(), track peak memory and decide where line length limits belong.

### Diagnose a counterexample
For Stream, write down the expected outcome, deliberately break an assumption from this specific example, and determine what must be checked at the boundary before this behavior could be reused safely.

## String

### Actual meaning
Ordered text representation. Python strings are sequences of Unicode code points, not raw UTF-8 bytes, and combining characters may affect visible character count.

### Concrete starting point
~~~text
text='Γεια'
assert len(text)==4
assert len(text.encode('utf-8'))>len(text)
~~~

### Apply the rule
Compare 'é' and 'e\u0301' before and after NFC normalization; record code points and encoded byte lengths.

### Diagnose a counterexample
For String, write down the expected outcome, deliberately break an assumption from this specific example, and determine what must be checked at the boundary before this behavior could be reused safely.

## Timeout

### Definitions
A timeout is a limit on waiting or computation. A connection timeout, idle-read timeout and total operation deadline are not the same. Expiration does not necessarily mean the remote server rolled back an operation; a payment or upload may have completed just before the client stopped waiting.

### Local process lab with controlled cleanup
