Record Java and build tool versions, original class name, deployment archive contents and classpath/module path. If changing packaging resolves the failure, prove it with the identical executable invoked under the corrected path.


### Termux: diagnose broken package repositories

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-ops-17-termux-repository-recovery.html

# Termux: recover package metadata without destroying the environment

## Capture the actual failure first
Run `termux-info` and record the application source, Android release and enabled repository URLs. Then use `pkg update` to reproduce the failure, keeping the first HTTP status, TLS error or signature message. “Unable to locate package” is not interchangeable with “repository has no Release file”: the former can mean a misspelled package name or a missing enabled component, while the latter concerns repository metadata. Preserve the output before changing configuration.

~~~sh
termux-info
pkg update
apt-cache policy python
~~~

## Decide which branch applies
For a DNS or timeout error, verify connectivity and whether the chosen mirror resolves; do not disable TLS verification. For a stale or retired mirror, use `termux-change-repo` to choose a currently maintained repository and then refresh metadata. For a signature or repository-origin change, read the complete warning; do not automatically trust an unexpected signing key. `pkg upgrade` changes installed packages and belongs **after** you understand the repair, not at the beginning of a blind recovery.

## An easily missed Android boundary
Do not mix app builds and add-ons signed by different publishers. A Termux APK installed through one distribution channel may be incompatible with plug-ins from another; check the publisher's official guidance before migration. Back up working project files and note the `PREFIX` value before reinstalling the application. Never replace all `sources.list` entries with an unverified mirror pasted from a random chat.

## Validate and stop
Refresh once with `pkg update`, inspect one known installed package with `pkg list-installed`, and test `python --version` if Python was already present. If network access remains broken, keep the observed error and investigate the network instead of repeatedly clearing APT's databases. This lesson does not claim a repair has been run on the reader's device.

Reference: https://github.com/termux/termux-packages/wiki/Package-Management


### Termux storage: shared folders, permissions and symlinks

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-ops-18-android-storage-and-symlinks.html

# Android storage is not an ordinary Linux home directory

## Two distinct namespaces
Termux's private `$HOME` and `$PREFIX` support executable scripts, permissions and Unix-style tools. Android shared storage, often reached through `$HOME/storage/shared`, is mediated by platform permissions and filesystem layers. Running source code or placing Unix sockets in shared storage can fail even when reading a photograph works. Keep active project repositories under `$HOME` and export finished media to shared storage when required.

~~~sh
printf 'HOME=%s\nPREFIX=%s\n' "$HOME" "$PREFIX"
pwd
ls -ld "$HOME" "$HOME/storage" "$HOME/storage/shared" 2>&1
stat "$HOME" 2>&1
~~~

## Establish access safely
`termux-setup-storage` requests the Android storage permission and sets up convenience paths where supported. A denied prompt must be fixed through Android's application permissions, not by giving every file mode 777. `ls -l` and `readlink` can identify symbolic links; a dangling path is different from a refused access operation. Shared folders may differ across Android versions, so treat their availability as an observation to confirm, not a guarantee.

## A small separation test
Create a harmless file inside a temporary project directory under `$HOME`, write one word and read it back. Then try copying that file into a user-approved shared folder. A failure only on the second operation points to storage access or filesystem behavior, not a broken Python installation. Record both paths, Android version and whether the permission prompt was accepted.

## Preservation rule
Never run recursive permission changes or deletion commands on all of `/storage` or `$HOME` to “fix access.” If an app must consume a file from Downloads, validate that path and copy only that file into its project-owned working directory. Avoid treating Android's scoped-storage boundaries as root access problems.


### Termux Python: pip, binary wheels and native-build failures

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-ops-19-pip-native-dependencies.html

# A failed pip install may be a platform compatibility problem

## Find out which interpreter and architecture are active
On Termux, packages distributed as prebuilt wheels for ordinary Linux desktop systems may not include a binary compatible with Android. The error may occur while selecting wheel tags or compiling a native extension; retrying with sudo is neither useful nor a supported Android recovery strategy. Inspect Python, pip and platform information before installing again.

~~~sh
python -c 'import sys,platform; print(sys.version); print(sys.executable); print(platform.machine())'
python -m pip --version
python -m pip debug --verbose
~~~

## Distinguish three failures
“No matching distribution” can arise from an unsupported Python version, a missing compatible platform wheel, or a package/version constraint. A failure while building a wheel usually includes actual compiler or header diagnostics. An import error after installation can instead mean a missing shared library or that a different interpreter is running. Preserve the first meaningful error lines and the exact requested version; don't silently replace them with random version downgrades.

## Reproduce with a disposable environment
Use a new directory under the private Termux home and check whether `python -m venv` works in that installation. A project-local venv can isolate Python packages, but cannot turn Android into glibc Linux. Inspect whether Termux's package repository already provides the relevant native component, and prefer maintained packages over arbitrary binaries. Verify license and provenance of any third-party build instructions before following them.

## Define success clearly
Installation succeeds only if a minimal `import` works and the desired API can execute with expected results. Record Python release, Android release, architecture, package version and the command that performed the successful check. If no compatible build exists, document that limitation instead of fabricating a successful install.

Official baseline: https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html
## Separate interpreter tags from platform compatibility

A wheel name includes interpreter, ABI and platform tags. Matching the CPU architecture alone is not sufficient: Android/Termux uses a different platform environment from ordinary glibc Linux. A Linux ARM wheel is not automatically a compatible Android package. The active Python executable and its build configuration are part of the evidence.

Before attempting a source build, record the interpreter, platform, package version and full compiler error. Distinguish a missing compiler from unavailable system headers and a project that assumes desktop-only APIs. Repeating pip install with administrative privileges does not solve an incompatible binary ABI.

```python
import platform, sys, sysconfig
facts = {"python":sys.version.split()[0], "machine":platform.machine(),
         "platform":sysconfig.get_platform(),
         "extension_suffix":sysconfig.get_config_var("EXT_SUFFIX")}
assert facts["python"] and facts["platform"]
print(facts)
```

The diagnostic runs on the current machine and does not claim that this machine is Android. Compare its output with the target phone before selecting packages. Preserve the first meaningful compiler error; the final “failed building wheel” line usually describes the outcome rather than the cause.

[Technical reference](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/platform-compatibility-tags/)


### Termux: background process, battery and interrupted jobs

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-ops-20-android-process-limits.html

# A long-running task can stop even if the program is correct

## Identify the kind of termination
Android manages background execution, battery optimization and app lifecycle separately from a traditional Linux server. If a build disappears after the screen locks, do not assume an uncaught Python exception. Record whether the terminal was disconnected, the process received a signal, the phone ran out of memory, or the OS restricted the application. A command killed by the OS might not get an opportunity to write its own error log.

~~~sh
printf 'shell pid: %s\n' "$$"
ps -ef | head -25
printf 'time: '; date -Is
printf 'HOME=%s\n' "$HOME"
~~~

## Prefer checkpointable work
For a multi-hour archive audit, split input into restartable batches and persist a small progress manifest after each *verified* stage. Use atomic file replacement for state files: write a new version in the same directory, flush where necessary, then rename. Never consider the presence of a half-written ZIP evidence that a backup finished. Keep intermediate data inside the app-private workspace and export the completed artifact once validation passes.

## Device settings are a diagnostic variable
Inspect battery restrictions for the Termux application and whether background execution is allowed in the installed Android version. A wake lock, where available through Termux support, concerns device sleep behavior; it is not unlimited permission to ignore Android lifecycle rules. Keeping the app foregrounded can help reproduce a problem but is not a universal stability guarantee.

## Acceptance test
Run a harmless job that writes numbered checkpoints, leave the device idle for a measured interval, and compare the last durable checkpoint with expected progress. Log the Android release, Termux build source and whether the process remained active. Do not disable all device security controls merely to run a test.
## Restartable work survives better than a persistent shell

A wake lock can keep a device awake in some situations, but it does not grant immunity from process termination, vendor restrictions or exhausted memory. Treat a long-running phone task as interruptible. Split work into independently identifiable items and persist acknowledgment only after an item's output is safely recorded.

If work is replayed after a restart, its identifier should prevent a duplicate effect. Merely remembering the last printed progress percentage is insufficient because terminal output and durable output can be at different boundaries. The fixture models repeated delivery with a set of completed item IDs.

```python
completed=set(); effects=[]
for item in ["a","b","a","c","b"]:
    if item in completed: continue
    effects.append(item)
    completed.add(item)
assert effects == ["a","b","c"]
print("replayed items suppressed")
```

This in-memory demonstration is not crash-safe storage. A real implementation must commit the output and acknowledgment together or make output replacement idempotent. Test termination between those two actions on disposable data, and report an interrupted job honestly instead of promising permanent background execution.

[Technical reference](https://github.com/termux/termux-app#installation)


### Termux proot: environment isolation and limits

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-ops-21-proot-container-limitations.html

# proot is a user-space compatibility layer, not a virtual machine

## Set correct expectations
A Linux distribution running through proot inside Termux can offer familiar directories, shells and package commands without Android root. It does not grant privileged kernel features, real container isolation, arbitrary mounts or systemd PID 1 semantics. A command that works on Ubuntu installed natively might fail under proot because access to devices and kernel interfaces remains governed by Android and the host application.

~~~sh
uname -a
id
pwd
cat /proc/1/comm 2>/dev/null || true
command -v systemctl || true
~~~

## Diagnose across both layers
When an executable is missing, check whether you are in native Termux or inside the guest distribution. Compare `command -v python`, `uname -m`, the package manager, and environment variables before installation. Errors opening `/dev` resources may be structural, not a reason to run the guest as root. A command like `systemctl` may exist but fail because a full service manager is not actually running as init.

## Keep work reproducible
Maintain sources in version control and a small file listing guest distribution, architecture and installed dependencies. Keep backups outside ephemeral guest directories. For development tools, prefer running only the build components that need the guest; accessing Android storage directly from the guest may require an explicitly supported bind or path mapping.

## Verification standard
Demonstrate a basic user-space command, a package lookup and a file read in the guest. Record any unsupported service/namespace operation as a platform limitation with the exact error rather than “missing permissions.” Do not suggest bypassing Android sandboxing to emulate unsupported kernel features.

## Three identities to record separately
A guest's displayed UID, the Android application's host UID and the device's kernel privileges are not interchangeable. A guest prompt saying root describes the environment presented to user-space programs; it does not grant Android root. Likewise, a guest package manager installs guest packages, while `pkg` in native Termux targets a different prefix and ABI environment.

## Trace an executable mismatch
Write down `command -v python`, the active shell and `uname -m` in both environments. A missing loader, an architecture mismatch and an absent command are distinct failures. Keep guest-created virtual environments with the guest interpreter that created them. Do not repair missing libraries by copying arbitrary `.so` files from the native Termux prefix into the guest.

## Boundary test for background work
Start a harmless short-lived command, observe its exit code, then compare a longer test when the Android app is backgrounded. The guest cannot guarantee survival against host process termination. Save progress incrementally and make a resumed operation idempotent, so restarting does not duplicate output. A guest service launcher can help a user-space daemon but does not establish a real booted systemd system.


### Linux permissions: diagnose DAC, ACLs and mount rules

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-ops-22-linux-permissions-acls.html

# Do not solve access failures by making everything world-writable

## Describe the exact operation
The operating system checks different privileges for reading a file, entering a directory, creating a new entry and executing a program. Begin with the failing filename, process identity and action; `ls -l` on the final file is incomplete if a parent directory lacks search permission. ACLs and mount flags can further constrain access even if ordinary mode bits appear correct.

~~~sh
id
namei -l ./example/path 2>/dev/null || true
ls -ld . ./example 2>/dev/null || true
findmnt -T . -o TARGET,FSTYPE,OPTIONS 2>/dev/null || true
~~~

## Separate authority from symptoms
A script can be readable and still fail direct execution on a `noexec` mount. A directory may permit listing but not traversal, depending on modes and ACLs. An executable invoked by an interpreter (for instance `python script.py`) follows different checks from `./script.py`. `getfacl` is useful if installed, but absence of that utility is not evidence no ACL exists.

## Controlled fixture
In a disposable directory belonging to you, create one regular text file and show read access. Then change only its permissions and compare `stat` and the result under the same user. Restore the original mode before finishing. Avoid using recursive `chmod -R 777`, global ownership changes or administrator execution as shortcuts.

## End with least privilege
The correct fix might be moving project output to a user-writable directory, granting a specific group read permission, or correcting a directory's ownership via the authorized administrator. Capture before/after results for the same operation and explain why broader permissions would be unnecessary.

## Directory permissions change the meaning of the operation
Reading a file checks its read permission plus traversal on parent directories. Creating or deleting a directory entry requires appropriate rights on the parent directory, not simply write permission on the file. Deleting a writable file and editing its bytes are different operations; sticky directories add further restrictions. ACL masks can reduce the effective rights of named users or groups, so inspect the effective result rather than adding mode bits at random.

## Reproducible permission experiment
In a new temporary directory, create `note.txt`, record its original mode, remove only its owner-read bit and attempt the same read under the same account. Restore the mode in a finally/cleanup path. If the test runs as root or with a relevant capability, it may still succeed: that is an account-context result, not proof that mode bits are irrelevant. Repeat as an ordinary account before drawing conclusions.

An interpreter reading `python note.py` is different from executing `./note.py`; the first still needs readable source and an executable interpreter. Neither pattern gives Android apps access outside their sandbox. On shared Android storage, place the project in Termux-private storage when it needs Unix execution or symlink behavior.


### Linux disk full: blocks, inodes and read-only mounts

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-ops-23-linux-disk-inodes-mounts.html

# Diagnose storage errors by errno and filesystem

## Space, quota and read-only access are different failures
A failed file creation is not enough to conclude that the drive is full. ENOSPC indicates unavailable filesystem space or metadata capacity; EDQUOT concerns an enforced quota; EROFS means the operation targets a read-only filesystem. EACCES instead concerns access permission. A read-only mount can have plenty of free blocks. Keep the exact exception before choosing a repair.

## Inspect the destination, not just the root filesystem
~~~sh
df -h .
df -i .
findmnt -T . -o TARGET,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
du -h -d 1 .
~~~
Use the directory actually receiving the output in place of `.`. The temporary directory used during packaging can be on a different mount from the final ZIP. `df -i` is meaningful only for filesystems that expose useful inode accounting. `findmnt` is a Linux utility; a missing command on Android does not prove the storage is healthy or unhealthy.

## A bounded write probe with an identifiable result
After inspecting the path, run this against a directory you control. It creates and removes one temporary file; it does not delete caches or existing documents.
~~~python
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import NamedTemporaryFile
import errno

target = Path('.')
try:
    with NamedTemporaryFile(dir=target, prefix='storage-probe-') as probe:
        probe.write(b'ok\n')
        probe.flush()
        print('write probe succeeded')
except OSError as exc:
    print(errno.errorcode.get(exc.errno, 'UNKNOWN'), exc.filename)
~~~
A successful small write only demonstrates that this operation worked at this time. It cannot prove that a large build will fit or that buffered data has survived a power loss. Reproduce the original operation after a narrowly chosen correction.

## Why du and df can disagree
`du` measures the files it can traverse; `df` reports filesystem accounting. Deleted files still held open by a process can consume space until the last descriptor closes. Snapshots, reserved blocks and container layers create further differences. Permission-denied messages during `du` make its total incomplete. Inspect the owning process before restarting it; deleting additional unrelated files does not address an open deleted file.

## Recovery decision
For block exhaustion, identify rebuildable output and estimate required headroom before removing it. For inode exhaustion, investigate unusually many small generated files. For EROFS following storage errors, preserve data and inspect kernel/storage diagnostics with the administrator; do not remount read-write as a blind first step. For quota exhaustion, free space elsewhere on the same disk may not change your allocation.

Reference: [Linux file-opening errors](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/open.2.html).
## Unlinked open files explain df/du disagreements

Removing a directory entry does not necessarily release the bytes immediately. An open file descriptor can keep an unlinked file alive until the last relevant reference closes. A filesystem-wide usage report may therefore count space that a directory walk cannot find by filename.

Diagnose which process owns the open handle before restarting anything. Do not truncate a descriptor belonging to an unknown service just to make a number smaller. The Linux fixture uses only a temporary file and proves that its contents remain readable through the already-open handle after unlinking.

```python
import os, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path=Path(folder)/"open.txt"
    path.write_bytes(b"still referenced")
    with path.open("rb") as stream:
        path.unlink()
        assert not path.exists()
        assert stream.read() == b"still referenced"
print("open handle retains data")
```

Run this on Linux or the private filesystem of Termux; file deletion rules differ on Windows. The tiny fixture does not measure reclaimed blocks. For an operational incident, compare mount scope, permissions and open-file evidence before concluding that filesystem accounting is broken.

[Technical reference](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/unlink.html)


### Linux networking: isolate DNS, routes, TLS and proxy errors

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-ops-24-linux-dns-and-tls.html

# A failed HTTPS download has multiple possible causes

## Test in layers, without bypassing certificates
Check whether the host name resolves, then whether a TCP connection can be made, then whether TLS validates the intended endpoint. An HTTP 404 or 403 means a server responded; it is not the same as a DNS failure. A proxy can change both the destination and certificate chain. Record the target host, timestamp and whether the failure affects one host or all destinations.

~~~sh
getent hosts example.org
ip route get 1.1.1.1 2>/dev/null || true
curl -I --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 12 https://example.org/
# Report proxy variable names only; use the Python check below.
~~~

## Interpret the evidence
DNS resolution with a failed route suggests connectivity or firewall issues. TCP connectivity with an unknown certificate authority points toward the trust store, a legitimate enterprise interception proxy or a misconfigured server. Clock drift can make valid certificates appear expired or not yet valid. Never use `curl -k` as a permanent fix: it suppresses the identity check that protects the connection.

## Compare controlled cases
Use a known public documentation host and your target host; if only one fails, examine destination-specific conditions before changing global DNS. Run a minimal `curl -I` rather than downloading unknown binaries. A 301 redirect is a normal HTTP outcome; follow the full chain only when you can inspect its destinations and policies.

## Verification record
Write down the resolved address, selected network interface, status or TLS diagnostic, certificate hostname and tool versions. The remediation could be a corrected URL, authorized proxy configuration, a synchronized clock or repaired CA bundle. Do not embed personal proxy credentials in a shared diagnostic report.

## Interpret exit status separately from HTTP status
With its default options, curl can finish a transfer successfully even when the server returns HTTP 404. The process exit status describes transfer/tool success; the HTTP response code describes the application response. Use `curl -I --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 12 --write-out '\nHTTP=%{http_code}\n' https://example.org/` to keep both visible. HEAD support varies; a server rejecting HEAD does not prove that GET is broken. Do not use that example to send requests to an arbitrary private target.

## Report proxy presence without printing credentials
Proxy URLs can contain passwords. Replace a complete environment dump with a name-only check:
~~~python
import os
for name in ('http_proxy', 'https_proxy', 'all_proxy', 'no_proxy',
             'HTTP_PROXY', 'HTTPS_PROXY', 'ALL_PROXY', 'NO_PROXY'):
    print(name, 'set' if os.environ.get(name) else 'unset')
~~~
This intentionally withholds proxy addresses and bypass lists. Review those values locally only if necessary. A proxy may resolve the destination itself, so local DNS success and proxy-side name resolution are not equivalent observations.

## Distinguish the failed layer
Record the first error: name lookup, connect timeout, connection refusal, TLS verification or HTTP status. A refusal can be produced by an endpoint or an intermediary; it does not identify the remote application's condition on its own. Certificate failures need the expected hostname, accurate device clock and intended trust chain. Do not disable verification to make the diagnostic look successful.

Tool reference: [curl manual](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html).


### Git recovery: reflog, detached HEAD and discarded changes

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-ops-25-git-recovery-before-reset.html

# Distinguish uncommitted edits from unreachable commits

## Inspect state before repair
`git status`, `git branch --show-current` and `git log --oneline --decorate -8` reveal three different facts: the working tree, selected branch and recent commit graph. A detached HEAD is valid when inspecting an older commit; it is not automatically data loss. If work was committed before an accidental reset, the local reflog may still reference it. Uncommitted edits are not generally recoverable through reflog.

~~~sh
git status --short
git branch --show-current
git log --oneline --decorate -8
git reflog -8
~~~

## Protect evidence before trying another reset
If an unexpected commit is visible in reflog, record its full SHA and inspect it with `git show --stat <sha>`. Create a recovery branch at that commit only after verifying it is the intended object. Avoid `git reset --hard` or `git clean -fd` until you know which tracked, ignored and untracked files they would affect. For an unsaved working tree, copy the entire project to another local directory first.

## A safe practice experiment
In a throwaway repository, create two commits on a topic branch and check out the earlier one. Observe detached HEAD, create another commit, then return to the original branch and examine reflog. You should be able to locate the detached commit by its SHA even if no branch currently points at it. Do not mistake this laboratory behavior for an unlimited guarantee: garbage collection and reflog expiry can make old objects unavailable.

## Done criteria
Record the lost change's original branch, whether it was committed, the recovery SHA, and the exact files verified after restoration. Pushing recovered history to a shared remote is a separate action requiring review; avoid rewriting collaborators' history simply to repair your local state.

## A recovery drill that does not discard work
Use an empty temporary directory. Configure a synthetic local Git identity there, create `note.txt` with `one`, add it and commit. Record that commit as A. Change the file to `two`, commit and record B. Run `git switch --detach A` using the recorded hash, create `detached.txt`, and commit it as C. Now `git switch -` can return to the preceding branch; `git reflog --date=iso -8` should show the detached commit.

Inspect C with `git show --stat C` and create `git branch recovered C`, substituting the actual hash. `git show recovered:detached.txt` should retrieve the committed content without checking out or replacing your current files. The drill requires no reset, clean, force push or remote repository.

## Uncommitted data needs a different recovery route
Reflog records movements of references in that local repository. It is not an automatic backup of unstaged file bytes, untracked files or work in another clone. Editor history, a filesystem backup, a previous stash or a copied working tree may help those cases. Inspect `git stash list` without assuming a stash exists. Protect any recovered files before attempting cleanup, and distinguish a branch name from the commit object it currently references.

Reference: [git reflog](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reflog).


### Python package mismatch: interpreter, pip, imports and ABI

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-ops-26-python-environment-forensics.html

# Installed is not the same as importable or runnable

## Trace the interpreter used by the failing command
A command launched by an IDE, scheduled task, shell alias or shebang may use a different Python than your terminal. First print `sys.executable`, the major/minor Python release and the location of the imported module. Use the **same** interpreter for `-m pip`; a bare `pip` on PATH can refer to a different installation.

~~~sh
python -c 'import sys,site;print(sys.executable);print(sys.version);print(site.getsitepackages())'
python -m pip --version
python -m pip show requests
python -c 'import importlib.util;print(importlib.util.find_spec("requests"))'
~~~

## Separate four diagnoses
ModuleNotFoundError may mean a package is absent in the active interpreter, that your project shadows its name, or that an optional import path is unavailable. ImportError can arise inside an installed package. A native extension may fail only at load time if its architecture or ABI does not match. `python -m pip check` checks declared dependency relationships but cannot certify that binary imports or APIs work on the target platform.

## Exercise with controlled shadowing
In a disposable folder, name a file `json.py` and attempt to run code importing Python's standard `json` module. Inspect the imported module's `__file__` when available. Rename that local file and remove only its own stale cache; do not delete the entire system cache. This demonstrates why working directory and filenames matter beyond package installation.

## Repair and acceptance
Choose the correct interpreter, use a project-local virtual environment where available, install declared dependencies from trusted sources, and run a minimal API call plus your project's tests. Capture OS, architecture, Python version and pip's reported version. A successful `pip install` is necessary for some repairs, but not proof the original application now works.


### Release archives: reproducibility, hashing and safe extraction

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-ops-27-reproducible-builds-and-zips.html

# A successful ZIP operation is not a verified release

## Define the source of truth
A release should record the exact source revision, license, dependency versions, target OS/architecture and command used for packaging. Collect files from an explicit allowlist rather than packaging every development cache and local credential. Normalize entry paths and preserve a clear top-level directory structure that works for Windows, Linux and Android ZIP viewers.

~~~sh
python -m compileall -q scripts
sha256sum release.zip
unzip -t release.zip
unzip -Z1 release.zip | head -30
~~~

## Threat model the archive itself
A ZIP can contain `../` entries, absolute paths, symlinks, duplicate filenames or huge compressed members. Verify the members before extracting untrusted archives. Never unzip unknown content directly into your home folder or a server document root. A SHA-256 digest detects changed bytes when compared to a trusted published checksum, but it does not establish who produced the release by itself.

## Make the build repeatable
Timestamps, file ordering and platform-dependent separators can change archive hashes between runs. Sort entries and use stable metadata when byte-for-byte reproducibility is required. Compare the final archive's manifest against actual filenames and record the exact Python/zip tooling version. Keeping only final files avoids publishing accidentally generated test data and authentication tokens.

## Acceptance exercise
Package two small sample files and compute their file hashes. Then make a fresh extraction into a disposable directory, validate expected content and try a second build from the same sources. State whether hashes match and why they might differ. Do not claim reproduction without recording both observed digests.
## Normalize archive metadata before comparing release hashes

Two ZIP files containing the same document text can have different hashes because entry order, timestamps, permissions or compression settings differ. Reproducibility requires controlling the packaging process as well as the source contents. Sort paths, choose a deliberate timestamp and document whether compression output is expected to remain identical across tool versions.

Use a temporary staging tree and never normalize timestamps by modifying the user's working files. The fixture creates two deterministic uncompressed archives in memory. It demonstrates byte reproducibility for this controlled recipe, not for every ZIP compressor.

```python
import io, zipfile, hashlib
def release():
    output=io.BytesIO()
    with zipfile.ZipFile(output,"w",compression=zipfile.ZIP_STORED) as z:
        for name,data in sorted({"b.txt":b"two", "a.txt":b"one"}.items()):
            entry=zipfile.ZipInfo(name,date_time=(2020,1,1,0,0,0))
            entry.create_system=3
            entry.external_attr=0o100644 << 16
            z.writestr(entry,data)
    return output.getvalue()
a,b=release(),release()
assert a == b
print(hashlib.sha256(a).hexdigest())
```

Change one input byte and verify that the release hash changes. Record toolchain and packaging settings next to the manifest. Reproducible packaging does not establish that an archive is safe to extract; path traversal and decompression limits remain separate checks.

[Technical reference](https://docs.python.org/3/library/zipfile.html)


### CI with limited minutes: local gates and release evidence

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-ops-28-ci-without-wasting-minutes.html

# Spend CI minutes on platform-dependent checks, not routine editing

## Build a validation pyramid
Cheap syntax, link, schema and duplicate checks belong in a local script that a contributor can run before committing. Integration tests should use small deterministic fixtures. Reserve GitHub-hosted workflows for tests requiring an environment you do not have locally, such as a clean runner, browser binary or packaging on another OS. A job that automatically succeeds after disabling a failing quality gate is not evidence of readiness.

~~~sh
python -m compileall -q scripts
python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p 'test_*.py'
python scripts/audit_offline_links.py
python scripts/audit_knowledge_depth.py --strict
~~~

## Preserve fault visibility
Make every required command return nonzero when it detects a violation; don't hide errors with `|| true` on release gates. If a staging-only audit is intentionally advisory, label its status separately from the production release decision. Do not launch expensive jobs for each one-line spelling correction: batch changes and run the complete suite at a meaningful checkpoint.

## Avoid dangerous automation side effects
Pin third-party actions to reviewed revisions where feasible, scope the workflow token to minimum permissions, and treat pull-request input as untrusted. Separate staging publishing from production credentials. For a private Test workflow, do not accidentally push edited source into another repository or publish a stale CNAME. Keep deployment manifest URLs tied to the selected target.

## Define a review record
Report the source commit, suite command, start/end time, platform, failed tests and artifact hashes. A green page deployment plus a red editorial audit is **not** a finished knowledge release. Keep a reproducible manual command for each CI job so spending the limited Actions allocation has a clear benefit.

Reference: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work


### Reverse engineering: inspect binary headers and bounded offsets

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-reverse-20-binary-header-validation.html

# Understand a binary structure before opening it in a disassembler

## Start with a synthetic file you own
A file signature is evidence of a possible format, not proof that all later fields are valid. Create a test fixture with a four-byte marker, an unsigned little-endian length and a UTF-8 payload. The fixed-width header is 8 bytes; an offset points to the first byte after that header. Never trust a declared payload size without checking how many bytes actually remain.

~~~python
from struct import pack, unpack_from
blob = b"DEMO" + pack("<I", 3) + b"cat"
assert blob[:4] == b"DEMO"
length = unpack_from("<I", blob, 4)[0]
assert length <= len(blob) - 8
assert blob[8:8+length] == b"cat"
~~~

## Generate two failure fixtures
Truncate the last byte and confirm a parser rejects the payload before attempting to decode it. Then replace the header length with a very large number; do not allocate that size. Checking the declared length against the actual file size prevents both out-of-range slicing assumptions and uncontrolled memory requests. A parser that returns an empty slice for invalid data may silently hide corruption.

## Separate observation from inference
In a hex viewer, record the first 16 bytes and mark each field's offset, width, signedness and byte order. If an unknown binary starts with ELF, PE or ZIP-like bytes, inspect it with a read-only tool appropriate for that format and compare the claim with actual structural offsets. Do not execute samples of unknown provenance just to “see what happens.”

## Lab deliverable
Produce a field table for the synthetic example, three fixture hashes, expected accept/reject results and a precise error code for truncation. A useful reverse-engineering note should include the bytes that support every structural claim, not simply identify a recognizable magic number.

## Turn observations into a parser contract
This format contains exactly one record. Reject a truncated header, a bad marker, a length beyond the byte buffer, invalid UTF-8 and trailing bytes. An upper size bound limits decoded text, but a file reader must also enforce its own input-byte limit before loading a large file.
~~~python
from struct import pack, unpack_from

def parse_record(blob):
    if len(blob) < 8:
        raise ValueError('short header')
    if blob[:4] != b'DEMO':
        raise ValueError('bad magic')
    length = unpack_from('<I', blob, 4)[0]
    if length > 1024 or length != len(blob) - 8:
        raise ValueError('invalid length')
    return blob[8:].decode('utf-8', errors='strict')

valid = b'DEMO' + pack('<I', 3) + b'cat'
assert parse_record(valid) == 'cat'
for broken in (b'', valid[:-1], valid + b'!',
               b'DEMO' + pack('<I', 2**32-1),
               b'DEMO' + pack('<I', 1) + b'\xff'):
    try:
        parse_record(broken)
    except (ValueError, UnicodeDecodeError):
        continue
    raise AssertionError('malformed record accepted')
~~~
The subtraction check `length != len(blob) - 8` happens only after proving the header exists. That ordering matters in languages with unsigned arithmetic, where subtracting eight from a shorter length can underflow. Python integers do not overflow, but the same file format can be implemented in a fixed-width language later.

## Byte lengths are not character counts
For `γάτα`, UTF-8 byte length and Python character count differ. Store the encoded byte length in the header and test the decoded string separately. A field table should distinguish offset 4 (where length is stored) from offset 8 (where payload begins), and record little-endian byte order. The parser contract above rejects padding; a format that permits multiple records needs a cursor and a different trailing-data policy.

Reference: [Python struct](https://docs.python.org/3/library/struct.html).


### ELF and PE inspection: sections, symbols and imports

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-reverse-21-elf-and-pe-read-only.html

# Observe an executable's structure without executing unknown code

## Choose the right host tool
Linux ELF binaries can be inspected with `file`, `readelf -h`, `readelf -S` and `readelf -s` without running the target. `objdump -p` can show dynamic dependencies when supported. On Windows PE executables, use a trusted PE inspection tool to read the DOS/PE signatures, image headers, sections and import table. A Linux `readelf` command is not a parser for PE files; format selection matters.

~~~sh
file ./known-good-sample
readelf -h ./known-good-sample
readelf -S ./known-good-sample
readelf -d ./known-good-sample 2>/dev/null || true
sha256sum ./known-good-sample
~~~

## Questions a section table can answer
A section header has a name, type, file offset, size and flags; file offsets differ from runtime virtual addresses. A program may be stripped of symbols yet remain executable. An imported library's presence suggests a dependency, not proof that a particular function executes in every run. The entry address is a starting point for analysis, not a guarantee of the first user-written source statement.

## Work with a sample you compiled
Build a two-function C program in a disposable directory, once with debugging information and once stripped. Compare section and symbol listings while leaving the source unchanged. Explain which names disappear and what machine-level structure remains. Keep compiler version and build flags in the report; differences may be toolchain-dependent.

## Safety and evidence
Don't upload proprietary binaries or third-party malware to public scanning services without permission. Avoid running an unknown binary. Record original SHA-256, CPU architecture, executable format and exactly which command produced each observation. If a field cannot be explained from the headers, label it a hypothesis requiring more evidence.

## File offsets, RVAs and virtual addresses are separate coordinates
A disassembler may display a loaded virtual address while a hex viewer displays a file offset. In PE, an RVA is relative to the image base. Mapping an RVA to file bytes requires the matching section and validation against its raw data extent; a zero-filled virtual tail need not exist in the file. In ELF, loader behavior is described by program headers, while section headers describe organization useful for linking and analysis. A section name alone is not an execution guarantee.

## Compare a native object and an executable you compile yourself
On Linux with a C compiler and binutils, save `int answer(void) { return 42; }` as `sample.c`. Compile `cc -c sample.c -o sample.o` and inspect `readelf -h sample.o`, `readelf -s sample.o` and `objdump -d sample.o`. This is a relocatable object, not a runnable program: there is no required main function or process entry point. Record the declared machine architecture and the symbol named answer.

Now add a main function in a separate disposable source file and link an executable. Compare program headers and relocation information without assuming identical addresses across builds. Optimization can inline or eliminate functions; stripping can remove names without removing executable behavior. Preserve compile flags beside the hash so the comparison has a reproducible basis.

Format reference: [Microsoft PE specification](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/debug/pe-format).
## Virtual addresses are not automatically file offsets

An address shown by a disassembler can refer to a loaded virtual address space, while a hex editor uses file offsets. Converting between them requires the relevant section or segment mapping. Subtracting an image base alone is not a universal file-offset formula.

Some mapped memory, such as zero-initialized data, has no corresponding stored payload bytes. Validate that an address lies inside the file-backed portion before reading. The fictional mapping below deliberately separates virtual size from stored size; it is a model, not a parser for every ELF or PE variation.

```python
def mapped_offset(address, virtual_start, file_start, stored_size, virtual_size):
    delta=address-virtual_start
    if delta < 0 or delta >= virtual_size: return None
    if delta >= stored_size: return None
    return file_start+delta
assert mapped_offset(0x1010,0x1000,0x200,0x40,0x80) == 0x210
assert mapped_offset(0x1060,0x1000,0x200,0x40,0x80) is None
assert mapped_offset(0x0fff,0x1000,0x200,0x40,0x80) is None
print("file-backed range checked")
```

Check bounds against the actual file length after conversion. Different format fields may use relative virtual addresses, absolute addresses or offsets; label them explicitly in notes. Load-time relocation and address randomization add another mapping layer when comparing runtime observations.

[Technical reference](https://refspecs.linuxfoundation.org/elf/gabi4+/ch5.pheader.html)


### JavaScript bundle analysis: imports, sinks and source maps

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-reverse-22-javascript-bundle-tracing.html

# Track behavior through a generated JavaScript bundle

## Begin with a legally inspectable sample
Use a small application you wrote with two ES modules: one exports a pure formatting function and the other adds a DOM event listener. Build it with a documented bundler and preserve the unminified sources, output bundle and optional source map. Minification may rename symbols, merge modules and reorder safe expressions; string-searching a function name is therefore an unreliable proof of whether behavior survived.

**format.mjs**

~~~javascript
export const label = (n) => `count=${Number(n)}`;
~~~

**ui.mjs**

~~~javascript
import {label} from './format.mjs';
document.querySelector('#count')?.addEventListener('click', () => {
  console.log(label(4));
});
~~~

## Map the data flow
Find the click handler registration, the call that transforms input, and the output sink (`console.log` here). Explain which value enters the function and what a visible click should emit. Compare the generated bundle before and after adding a second module. A source map may help correlate positions but is optional and can expose original filenames; inspect it locally before distributing it.

## Four investigation pitfalls
Not seeing a readable import statement after bundling does not mean the import was removed. Dead-code elimination can omit unreferenced branches. A dynamic import may create a separate chunk. A minified symbol with a familiar name does not establish program intent without call-site evidence. Do not inject code into a third-party service or intercept user sessions to confirm a hypothesis.

## Acceptance evidence
Keep a small graph: entry module → handler → transformation → sink, with output-file offsets or line ranges. Test the click inside your own app, verify the expected message, and document whether tree shaking changes the bundle. Never present an inferred dependency graph as observed runtime execution without a run trace.


### Android APK inspection: manifest, assets and signatures

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-reverse-23-apk-read-only-inspection.html

# APK static inspection does not require installing the package

## Treat the package as untrusted input
An APK is ZIP-compatible for many of its contents, but executable resources and signing blocks require format-aware tools. Start with an app you built yourself or are authorized to examine. Record its SHA-256 and use a listing command to inventory paths before extraction. A manifest visible inside the archive may be binary XML, so a generic text editor cannot reliably decode it.

~~~sh
sha256sum sample.apk
unzip -l sample.apk | head -45
unzip -t sample.apk
# When Android SDK build-tools are installed:
apksigner verify --verbose sample.apk
~~~

## Distinguish what each result demonstrates
The archive test checks ZIP member integrity, not Android signing correctness. `apksigner verify` checks applicable APK signature schemes when the SDK tool is available; it does not certify app safety. The AndroidManifest declares requested permissions and components, but declarations alone don't prove those capabilities were exercised. App assets and resources can reveal filenames and UI structure without showing all runtime behavior.

## A bounded lab
Create a trivial “hello” Android application in a disposable development project. Compare the debug and release APK metadata and verification results. Record target SDK, min SDK, package name, signing certificate fingerprint and observed permissions. Never publish the private signing key or claim that a signature match guarantees a publisher is trustworthy.

## Analysis boundary
Do not modify a third-party APK to bypass purchases, authentication or access restrictions. In an authorized audit, report unexpected exported components or sensitive asset disclosures to the owner, with reproduction limited to your own test environment.

Reference: https://source.android.com/docs/security/features/apksigning


### PCAP triage: ports, flows, DNS and timing evidence

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-reverse-24-pcap-protocol-triage.html

# Network captures contain evidence and potentially private information

## Prefer a synthetic capture
Build a local client/server exchange or use a published training capture with explicit permission. A packet capture can contain IP addresses, hostnames, tokens, chat text or session identifiers; never send raw enterprise/customer traffic to a public service without approval. Begin by recording capture time zone, interface and whether packets were truncated at collection.

~~~sh
capinfos training.pcapng 2>/dev/null || true
tshark -r training.pcapng -q -z conv,tcp
tshark -r training.pcapng -Y 'dns' -T fields -e frame.time_epoch -e dns.qry.name
~~~

## Follow a flow, not merely a port number
A TCP connection can carry an unexpected application protocol; port 443 suggests TLS/HTTPS but doesn't prove it. Inspect protocol dissection, handshakes, timing and payload visibility. TLS encryption limits what a passive capture reveals about application content. Missing packets or capture filters can create false narratives about retransmission and server failure.

## Example question: was DNS the bottleneck?
Pair the client's DNS query and response where visible, compare the timestamp to the subsequent connection attempt, and identify whether the response was cached or a new lookup occurred. A failed domain resolution may precede no TCP connection at all. By contrast, a completed DNS response followed by SYN retransmissions points elsewhere. Distinguish relative time in the capture from a wall-clock timestamp.

## Audit artifact
Document filters, exact frames supporting the observation, packet loss caveats, and relevant endpoint addresses anonymized for sharing. Treat capture display filters as ways to **inspect** evidence, not proof that filtered-out packets never existed.
## Capture order, protocol sequence and observation gaps

Packet timestamps describe the capture point's observation, not a universal ordering of application events across hosts. Clock skew, buffering, retransmission and missing packets can change the apparent story. Keep original packet indices and capture metadata when sorting a timeline.

An absent response in one capture is evidence of non-observation at that capture point. It does not by itself prove that the remote application never replied. The fixture merges synthetic observations and preserves source identity so equal timestamps remain explainable.

```python
observations=[{"time":10,"source":"left","packet":2},
              {"time":9,"source":"right","packet":1},
              {"time":10,"source":"left","packet":1}]
timeline=sorted(observations,key=lambda r:(r["time"],r["source"],r["packet"]))
assert [(r["source"],r["packet"]) for r in timeline] == [("right",1),("left",1),("left",2)]
assert len(timeline) == len(observations)
print(timeline)
```

The tie-breaker provides deterministic display, not a claim of causal order. In real evidence, record capture interface, time resolution, drop counters and any clock correction. Restrict collection to traffic you are authorized to inspect and remove identifying payloads from teaching examples.

[Technical reference](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/wsug_html_chunked/ChAdvTimestamps.html)


### Reverse engineering evidence ledger and version diffing

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-reverse-25-evidence-ledger-and-diff.html

# A good technical finding can be reproduced by someone else

## Use an evidence ledger
For each conclusion record an identifier, source hash, tool and version, inspected byte/line range, direct observation, interpretation and confidence level. Keep observation separate from hypothesis. “The binary imports a network library” is an observation; “the feature sends private data” is a behavioral inference requiring runtime evidence and permission to investigate.

~~~text
E-001 | sha256=... | tool=readelf | section=.dynsym | observed=import name
H-001 | based-on=E-001 | interpretation=possible network feature
T-001 | owner-approved test | result=not executed / observed ...
~~~

## Compare like with like
When inspecting two builds, hash both originals, record architecture and compiler configuration, and compare stable structures such as symbols, strings, manifests or schema. Timestamp changes, debug symbols and compiler optimizations can produce large binary differences without a corresponding user-visible behavior change. A source-level change is not automatically the cause of every changed byte.

## Control the experiment
Change one feature in a program you own and produce builds A and B using the same toolchain. Record one changed source line and predict what will differ. Compare strings and dynamic symbols, then describe unexpected unrelated changes rather than hiding them. Repeat the build with no source change to measure nondeterministic output.

## Ethical boundary and handoff
An authorized security review should include reproduction steps that do not expose sensitive user information, affected version, remediation suggestion and a responsible disclosure path. If you cannot show a causal link between evidence and claim, downgrade the claim to “possible” and list what additional observation is required.


### Safe archive inspection: nested files, symlinks and size limits

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-reverse-26-safe-archive-forensics.html

# Inspect archives as structured data before extraction

## Enumerate without trusting file names
An archive entry's stored name may contain parent traversal `../`, absolute paths, repeated names or platform-specific separators. The declared uncompressed size can be enormous relative to its compressed size. Before accepting an unknown ZIP, set limits for file count, total uncompressed bytes and per-entry size; normalize names without permitting escape from the destination.

~~~python
from pathlib import PurePosixPath
names = ["docs/readme.txt", "../outside.txt", "/absolute/config"]
for name in names:
    parts = PurePosixPath(name.replace("\\", "/")).parts
    safe = not name.startswith(("/", "\\")) and ".." not in parts
    print(name, safe)
~~~

## Detect collisions before writing
Files named `A.txt` and `a.txt` may collide on case-insensitive systems. Repeated paths in one archive might be interpreted differently by different extractors. Symlink targets can point outside the extraction root even when entry names look harmless. A content scanner must consider the *resolved destination* and refuse unsupported link types, not merely strip `../` from suspicious strings.

## Use a deliberately hostile fixture
Create a tiny ZIP whose members include one safe path, one traversal path and two case-colliding names, without extracting it to a real project. Build a validator that returns a structured list of rejected entries. The expected behavior is fail-closed on the entire archive or quarantined extraction under a deliberately safe policy, not silently writing some unsafe members.

## Success boundaries
Document each configured limit and verify that zero bytes are written outside a disposable extraction root. A valid CRC does not prove a safe filename, acceptable decompressed size or trustworthy publisher. Keep the test archive alongside a hash and the expected rejection report.


### Threat modeling an offline-first static learning site

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-security-14-threat-model-for-offline-website.html

# A static website still processes untrusted data

## Draw the actual trust boundaries
An offline learning portal reads Markdown text, imported JSON/JavaScript indexes, browser preferences and links. The content repository is trusted only after review; third-party snippets, remote links and localStorage values can be malformed or hostile. Model the flow: source archive → curation → website build → browser rendering → optional external URL. Every boundary must identify who controls the data and what action consumes it.

~~~text
Author files -> indexed JSON -> HTML renderer -> DOM
Browser preferences -> display theme / language
External link -> user leaves trusted origin
Build credentials -> deployment service only
~~~

## Two meaningful attacker stories
If Markdown is rendered as unsanitized HTML, a malicious title or code block may inject executable script. If absolute URLs are hard-coded to production, a Test/backup build can send users to the wrong domain and leak environment context. Test escaping with a harmless marker that contains `<script>` as **text**, and assert it stays visible text rather than running. Verify generated canonical/OG URLs for each deployment separately.

## Reduce blast radius
Keep dangerous HTML escaping inside the renderer, restrict externally loaded scripts, never embed tokens in static assets and require least-privilege CI credentials. Treat package upgrades and documentation imports as supply-chain changes. Store no real personal data in example fixtures; provide synthetic cases that can be shared publicly.

## Acceptance record
For each trust boundary list input, possible failure, observable test, control and residual risk. The site is not “secure” merely because it has no backend; browser XSS, malicious downloads, dependency compromise and misleading links still matter.


### Secret exposure in source control: rotation and impact scope

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-security-15-secrets-incident-response.html

# Removing a token from the latest commit is not enough

## Establish whether a credential was exposed
If a token, password or private key was committed or embedded in an uploaded ZIP, treat it as potentially compromised until you can show otherwise. Record the affected repository, revision range, credential type and current permissions without copying the secret into logs or bug reports. First identify its issuing provider and owners so a revocation does not unexpectedly break unrelated production services.

~~~sh
git status --short
git log --oneline -8
# Review filenames and changes, not actual secret values:
git log --name-status --oneline -8
~~~

## Rotate before attempting history surgery
Revoke or rotate the credential through the actual provider, then update every service that depended on it through a secure configuration channel. Removing a line from Git does not invalidate an already copied key. History rewriting can reduce accidental discovery but requires collaborator coordination, backup analysis and careful force-push planning; it must never replace revocation.

## Evaluate scope with evidence
Determine whether the exposed credential had read-only or administrative privileges, whether it reached public artifacts and whether the provider can supply relevant access audit logs. Separate confirmed use from possible use: absence of visible events in a limited log is not proof nobody accessed a public token. Do not publish any realistic secret as an educational example.

## Prevent the next incident
Add structured secret scanning, `.gitignore` for local `.env` files, least-privilege short-lived credentials and a release manifest that rejects sensitive patterns. Verify the rotated service works, then document the incident without secret contents or personal identifiers.
## Rotation evidence must include consumers and revocation

Creating a replacement secret is only one step of rotation. Identify consumers, distribute the replacement through an approved channel, confirm that required services use it and revoke the exposed value. A long overlap window can leave the incident open even while the new value is working.

History cleanup reduces accidental future discovery but cannot retract copies already fetched by others. Do not use deletion of a source line as evidence that a credential is safe. Keep incident notes focused on secret identifiers and timestamps, never the secret values themselves.

```python
incident={"replacement_created":True,"consumers_verified":False,
          "old_revoked":False,"scope_reviewed":True}
def rotation_complete(row):
    return all(row[k] for k in ("replacement_created","consumers_verified","old_revoked","scope_reviewed"))
assert not rotation_complete(incident)
incident.update(consumers_verified=True,old_revoked=True)
assert rotation_complete(incident)
print("completion requires revocation evidence")
```

The Boolean model is a checklist fixture, not a credential-management service. Test the old credential against the documented provider verification mechanism without printing it. If exposure scope is uncertain, record that uncertainty and continue the investigation rather than inventing a clean bill of health.

[Technical reference](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html)


### Software supply-chain review: licenses, hashes and SBOM

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-security-16-dependency-provenance-sbom.html

# A dependency inventory is actionable only when tied to a build

## Capture exact versions and origin
A requirements file with loose package constraints expresses intent, not the precise environment installed today. Record resolved versions, source package URLs or registries, supported platforms and dependency licenses. For a Python project, `python -m pip freeze` provides a quick environment snapshot but may include undeclared transitives and local experiments; compare it with the application's actual lockfile and clean test install.

~~~sh
python -m pip list --format=json
python -m pip check
python -m pip freeze
sha256sum dist/package.whl 2>/dev/null || true
~~~

## Understand what a hash protects
A digest guards against a change **relative to a trusted known value**. It does not reveal whether the original dependency was malicious or licensed for your distribution. SBOM records components and relationships; it can support vulnerability queries and license review, but it is not a security certification. A build attestation links an artifact to particular workflow claims, which must still be validated and trusted.

## Mini-review exercise
Pick a harmless open-source library already in your own project. Find its upstream package name, declared license, exact installed version, transitive dependencies and where it appears in your release. Explain whether its license notice needs shipping with the binary or website. Record one scenario where the package is unnecessary so removing it reduces attack surface and maintenance.

## Release decision
Block publication if an unknown license or unreviewed binary enters a distribution, and document why any exception was approved. Never automatically substitute similarly named packages found on an arbitrary registry. Keep a dated inventory because dependency metadata and known vulnerabilities change over time.

Source: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/artifact-attestations


### Defensive web input handling and DOM output encoding

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-security-17-web-input-output-contracts.html

# Validate values for their meaning and encode for their destination

## Two different questions
Input validation asks whether a value belongs to the application's permitted domain; output encoding protects the interpreter in which it will be displayed. A product quantity may be restricted to a finite integer within a range, while a free-form user label is allowed to contain punctuation. Escaping input globally is not a substitute for encoding output for HTML, URLs or JavaScript contexts.

~~~javascript
function acceptQuantity(value) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(value) || value < 0 || value > 9999)
    throw new RangeError('quantity out of range');
  return value;
}
const label = '<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>';
const target = document.createElement('span');
target.textContent = label; // visible text, not parsed markup
~~~

## Understand where errors arise
`textContent` is appropriate for plain text; `innerHTML` interprets markup and can be dangerous with untrusted strings. URL handling needs schemes and destinations validated independently from HTML escaping. JSON parsing ensures syntax but not business constraints: a parsed object can still be missing required keys or contain the wrong type.

## Local demonstration
Create a tiny page with the code above, insert the target span into an owned DOM fixture and verify the literal angle brackets appear as text. Then test `acceptQuantity(0)`, `acceptQuantity(-1)`, and `acceptQuantity('4')`; only the nonnegative integer should pass. In production, define an actual schema and avoid relying on JavaScript implicit numeric coercion.

## Boundary statement
This exercise illustrates safe output handling, not a complete XSS prevention program. Real systems need an appropriate renderer, trusted dependencies, CSP where suitable, link validation and defense-in-depth around all HTML-producing paths.


### Python: unit tests, fixtures and regression boundaries

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-language-5-pytest-fixtures.html

# Python testing: prove behavior with small independent fixtures

## The contract and its boundary
Consider a function that converts a user quantity into a nonnegative integer. Define the accepted domain before writing tests; parsing an arbitrary string is not the same as validating a quantity. Make invalid inputs raise a specific exception instead of returning a number that silently changes meaning. Tests should assert behavior, not implementation details such as local variable names.

~~~python
import pytest

def quantity(value):
    if isinstance(value, bool) or not isinstance(value, int):
        raise TypeError('integer required')
    if value < 0:
        raise ValueError('negative quantity')
    return value

@pytest.mark.parametrize('value', [0, 1, 999])
def test_accepts_int(value):
    assert quantity(value) == value

def test_rejects_bool():
    with pytest.raises(TypeError):
        quantity(True)

def test_rejects_negative():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        quantity(-1)
~~~

## Why the bool case matters
Python's bool subclasses int, so a naive `isinstance(True, int)` check accepts True as 1. If your data contract requires actual numerical quantities rather than flags, explicitly reject it. A property-based test can explore many values, but targeted boundary cases document the intended behavior for future maintainers.

## Separate unit tests from environment tests
The test above makes no network calls and modifies no persistent files. A test of filesystem import paths, real services or interpreter ABI belongs in another test layer with controllable setup. For tests involving temporary files, use pytest's `tmp_path` fixture to avoid changing the developer's current directory. Pin test dependencies and run the suite with the same interpreter as the application.

## Proof of completion
Before changing the validation rule, add a failing test that captures the new edge case. After the fix, demonstrate red → green and show exact test output, Python version and pytest version. No execution is claimed for the reader's platform by the text of this lesson.


### JavaScript: fetch timeouts, abort and HTTP error handling

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-language-5-async-fetch-timeout.html

# A resolved fetch promise is not always an HTTP success

## Model transport and application failures separately
`fetch()` rejects for certain network or abort failures, but a 404 or 500 HTTP response usually fulfills the promise with `ok === false`. Always check status before assuming valid application data. A timeout should abort the request and its resources; adding a timer without an AbortController can leave unwanted work running.

~~~javascript
async function getJSON(url, ms = 3000) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), ms);
  try {
    const response = await fetch(url, {signal: controller.signal});
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
    return await response.json();
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}
~~~

## Classify a failure correctly
A JSON parse error means the response bytes were not accepted as JSON; it is different from an HTTP 503. Aborts, offline status and DNS failures may present different exceptions across browsers. Do not catch every exception and return an empty object, because that turns a temporary outage into misleading “no results.” Handle a cancellation initiated by the user differently from a retryable server error.

## Create a local deterministic server fixture
Provide `/ok` returning JSON, `/missing` returning 404 and `/slow` delaying beyond the timeout in a test server you control. Record three outcomes: object result, explicit HTTP error, and aborted fetch. Compare what the browser Network panel shows with the application's error message. Never use a public service as a repeated delay test without permission.

## Retry boundaries
GET requests are commonly repeatable, but requests with side effects need idempotency and deduplication by the server before automatic retries. Use bounded retry counts and backoff; an unlimited retry loop can amplify an outage. Add telemetry only if it avoids exposing URL query secrets or user-provided private data.
## Cancellation ownership and response-body completion

A fetch promise can resolve after response headers arrive while the body is still streaming. If a timeout is cleared immediately after fetch resolves, a later body read can remain unbounded. Keep the cancellation owner alive until the required body operation finishes. Also distinguish a rejected transport promise from an HTTP error response: a 404 is still an HTTP response that needs an explicit status decision.

Cancellation should propagate from the feature that owns the request. Replacing a search query should cancel the obsolete request, but an old rejection must not erase the newer result. The local fixture demonstrates ownership state without contacting a server.

```javascript
let current = 0;
function begin() { const version = ++current; return value => version === current ? value : null; }
const oldResult = begin();
const newResult = begin();
if (oldResult("old") !== null || newResult("new") !== "new") throw Error("stale result accepted");
const controller = new AbortController();
controller.abort();
if (!controller.signal.aborted) throw Error("cancellation not observable");
console.log("stale response ignored");
```

For the real client, test cancellation during headers and during body consumption separately. Bound decoded response size as well as elapsed time. A timeout does not undo a server-side write; retrying a cancelled write requires the same idempotency analysis as any uncertain response.

[Technical reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController)


### Bash: quoting, safe filenames and predictable failures

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-language-5-paths-and-safe-shell.html

# Shell scripts break when they confuse text with command syntax

## Treat every filename as arbitrary data
A path can contain spaces, asterisks or a leading dash. Unquoted variable expansion can split words and expand globs, silently changing which files a command touches. Always quote substitutions representing a single path. The `--` separator can protect many commands from confusing a filename beginning with `-` for an option.

~~~bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
root="${1:?provide an existing directory}"
if [[ ! -d "$root" ]]; then
  printf 'not a directory: %s\n' "$root" >&2
  exit 2
fi
root="$(cd -- "$root" && pwd -P)"
find "$root" -maxdepth 1 -type f -print0 |
while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
  printf 'file: %q\n' "$file"
done
~~~

## Why the NUL delimiter matters
A newline is legal inside a Unix filename, so line-based parsing can be ambiguous. `-print0` and `read -d ''` preserve exact boundaries. Never attempt to fix unusual filenames by running uncontrolled renaming over a user's data. The code above lists paths only; it does not remove or modify them.

## Know the limitations of strict mode
`set -e` behaves differently inside conditionals, pipelines and command substitutions; don't assume it guarantees transaction-like rollback. `pipefail` helps propagate pipeline failures, but a background process still needs explicit waiting and status checks. Use a small test suite with an empty directory, a path containing spaces and a path containing a newline.

## Expected evidence
The same files should be printed exactly once regardless of their names. Record Bash version and host OS; not all shells support `read -d` or the same `[[ ... ]]` syntax. Do not copy a Bash-specific script into generic POSIX sh without reviewing differences.

## Include option-like directory arguments in the test
Quoting preserves one argument but does not stop a program from interpreting a leading dash as an option. The `find` starting point in this lesson is normalized below to an absolute directory, so a caller can supply a directory whose name begins with `-`. The `--` used by `cd` belongs to Bash's builtin; support for that marker must be checked separately for other tools.

For a bounded exercise, create an empty temporary directory with files named `two words.txt`, `star*.txt` and a filename containing a newline. The output is shell-escaped presentation from `%q`, not a reversible line-based interchange format unless it is parsed with the same Bash rules. Do not feed that display back into `eval`. If another program consumes the result, retain NUL delimiters instead.

## A pipeline is not a transaction
If a consumer exits early, an upstream producer may fail with SIGPIPE. With pipefail, that can make the whole pipeline fail even though the intended first result was consumed. Check the status that corresponds to your contract rather than adding `|| true` everywhere. Files already written before a later error remain written. Temporary output plus a deliberate final rename is a separate design, not a feature supplied by `set -e`.

Reference: [Bash word splitting](https://www.gnu.org/s/bash/manual/html_node/Word-Splitting.html).
## Pipeline status and deliberate error handling

A pipeline normally reports the exit status of its last command. An earlier stage can fail while the final formatter exits successfully. Bash pipefail changes the pipeline status, but it does not replace a decision about which statuses are expected. Tools such as grep use distinct codes for “no match” and a real error, so a blanket failure policy can reject valid empty results.

The local fixture uses a deliberately failing producer and a successful consumer. It examines status directly instead of treating set -e as a complete exception system. Be especially explicit around conditionals, subshells and cleanup traps.

```bash
set -u
set +o pipefail
(exit 7) | cat >/dev/null
normal=$?
set -o pipefail
(exit 7) | cat >/dev/null
strict=$?
[[ "$normal" == 0 && "$strict" == 7 ]] || exit 1
printf 'pipeline statuses: %s %s\n' "$normal" "$strict"
```

Test an empty search result separately from an unreadable input file. Save a status immediately before another command overwrites it. For filenames read from a process, retain NUL separation where supported; newline-delimited paths are ambiguous when a filename itself contains a newline.

[Technical reference](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Pipelines.html)


### Rust: ownership and safe input parsing

Source-URL: https://ded-sec.space/learn/en/expanded-en-language-5-ownership-parsing.html

# Borrowing prevents some lifetime errors, not invalid business data

## Parse without panicking on user input
Use a function returning `Result` rather than calling `unwrap()` on an unknown string. The caller must decide whether a parse failure is recoverable. Accepting `i32` or `u32` changes the admissible set of numbers; choose the type according to the domain, not just to silence compiler diagnostics.

~~~rust
fn parse_port(input: &str) -> Result<u16, String> {
    let value: u16 = input.parse().map_err(|_| "not a valid port".to_owned())?;
    if value == 0 { return Err("port zero not allowed here".to_owned()); }
    Ok(value)
}
fn main() {
    assert_eq!(parse_port("8080"), Ok(8080));
    assert!(parse_port("70000").is_err());
    assert!(parse_port("0").is_err());
}
~~~

## Trace the ownership model
The function borrows `&str` and returns a new owned String only on error. It does not need to clone the input to parse its digits. The returned `u16` is a small copyable value; there is no dangling reference to the original string. If this API returned `&str` referencing a temporary local String, the borrow checker would reject the lifetime mismatch.

## Separate compiler rules from runtime behavior
Rust prevents classes of memory misuse with types and lifetimes, but does not make every parser semantically correct. A high-value test checks valid boundaries, overflow, leading/trailing whitespace policies and application-specific constraints. Record whether `cargo test` actually ran on the selected toolchain.

## Exercise
Change the domain to include port zero and update the tests before code. Explain why the compiler accepts the original function yet the business requirement changes. Investigate what happens for `" 8080 "` and document whether trimming is a desired feature or an unexpected input acceptance.
## Byte offsets versus UTF-8 character boundaries
